Following an embarrassing 31-14 loss at Utah State, Jim Mora unleashed a fiery postgame tirade unlike anything we've heard from a CSU head coach in years. He called out his players, coaching staff, the program's culture, and even the university itself, declaring that "the hammer is coming down." Joel and Mike dissect Mora's explosive comments, revisit the baffling decision to retain former defensive coordinator Tyson Summers, and explore whether deeper issues behind the scenes could be complicating CSU's rebuild. Plus, a brief look ahead to a daunting matchup with Boise State and the start of CSU basketball season.

Colorado State.title: A defensive disaster: CSU gets embarrassed on Homecoming, Tyson Summers is out
Colorado State.summary:
What should have been a celebration turned into another nightmare for CSU football. A record 41,000 fans packed Canvas Stadium for Homecoming and the Rams’ first Pac-12 conference game, only to watch Oregon State roll up 650 yards without punting once in a 56-26 rout. Joel and Mike break down another historically bad defensive performance before diving into the biggest story of the weekend: Jim Mora stripping defensive coordinator Tyson Summers of play-calling duties mid-game, Summers leaving the sideline, and his subsequent dismissal from the program. Was the change overdue? And, why did Mora allow the defense to reach this point in the first place? The guys examine Summers’ surprising retention from the previous staff, Mora’s own responsibility for CSU’s three-game collapse, and whether new play-caller Kenny McClendon can use the bye week to finally make this defense remotely competent.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Chauncey Wiggins earns preliminary injunction, set to debut against LSU
Gonzaga.summary:
Expressionless for more than an hour, Chauncey Wiggins finally exhaled, closing his eyes as he tilted his head back and processed four months of emotions.

“Really just took a deep breath and said, ‘Thank you, God,’ about 20 times,” Wiggins said.

Spokane Superior Court Judge Dean Chuang granted a temporary injunction to the Gonzaga forward on Thursday afternoon - a ruling that allows Wiggins to suit up for the 14th-ranked Bulldogs this season and, by all accounts, signals the end of a roller-coaster eligibility saga for the 6-foot-11 transfer.

Wiggins, who was ineligible for season-opening wins over Purdue and New Mexico State last week, said he expects to debut for Gonzaga on Saturday in a high-profile nonconference matchup with LSU (12:30 p.m., USA Network) at Numerica Veterans Arena, just a few-hundred yards from the fourth-floor courtroom where the player’s injunction hearing took place Thursday.

“I had a lot of faith, a lot of positivity,” Wiggins said. “That’s how I live my life, so I was just really hopeful and very positive of the attorneys and lawyers and the judge. So I’m just really thankful for everybody.”

More than two-dozen people attended Wiggins’ afternoon hearing, including Gonzaga coach Mark Few and teammates Braden Huff, Davis Fogle, Xaivian Lee, Javon Bennett, Parker Jefferson and Alonzo Metz. Wiggins wasn’t scheduled to appear in court until next Tuesday, but with Saturday’s Gonzaga-LSU matchup in mind, the player’s attorneys filed for a motion to shorten time, moving the hearing up by five days.

Wiggins maintained an optimistic outlook, even at points when the 21-year-old’s chances of obtaining a fifth season appeared grim.

After playing three years at Clemson and spending the 2025-26 season at Florida State, Wiggins joined the Boston Celtics at NBA Summer League but didn’t sign a professional contract, allowing him to explore fifth-year eligibility options. Around the same time, dozens of athletes across different states and sports - including Gonzaga’s Lee and Bennett - filed lawsuits against the NCAA, claiming they should be entitled to a fifth year of competition through the regulatory body’s new 5-in-5 eligibility model.

Wiggins initially joined the Godfrey v. NCAA lawsuit in his home state of Georgia - a 5-in-5 case originally filed by former Clemson teammate and current Arizona forward RJ Godfrey. A Cobb County judge granted an injunction to the plaintiffs, but the Court of Appeals stayed the case, reversing the decision and keeping Wiggins ineligible. Wiggins bailed on the Georgia lawsuit when oral arguments were scheduled for Jan. 12, 2027 - effectively sidelining the forward through Gonzaga’s first 15 games - and joined the Wheeler v. NCAA 5-in-5 lawsuit based in Waco, Texas, hoping for a better outcome.

It ultimately backfired when a McLennan County judge ruled Wiggins and other new plaintiffs had “a lack of personal jurisdiction” in the suit, denying the request for a temporary restraining order one day after Gonzaga’s Nov. 2 opener against Purdue.

That brought Wiggins’ eligibility battle to Spokane for a third, and possibly final, shot at an injunction.

Chuang, a Gonzaga Law graduate, listened to arguments from Wiggins’ attorney, Ryan Downton of the Texas Trial Group, and NCAA attorneys David Zeitlin and Taylor Askew - all three of whom appeared virtually via Zoom.

A crux of Downton’s argument pertained to the NCAA Manual and language of a specific bylaw that doesn’t explicitly state class of 2022 high school graduates are excluded from the 5-in-5 model.

“If it was truly an error that the manual was supposed to exclude these athletes, then they would’ve gotten together with their Cabinet, they would’ve taken a vote on it and they would’ve voted to change the language of the manual,” Downton said. “… They haven’t done that and what you’re left with is unambiguous text that makes Mr. Wiggins eligible.”

Arguing on behalf of the NCAA, Askew claimed “everybody has to be operating under the same set of standards,” and argued that while dozens of fifth-year athletes are currently competing under injunctions, “that doesn’t mean it’s fair.”

The defense also raised concerns about equity and opportunities eliminated by allowing class of 2022 graduates to return for a fifth season. Askew specifically referenced controversy surrounding North Carolina’s women’s field hockey team, which had a losing record before three fifth-year players were granted midseason injunctions, allowing the Tar Heels to win three of their last four contests and claim a spot in the NCAA Tournament, subsequently knocking ACC rival Wake Forest out of the bracket.

“That’s not fair,” Askew said. “These players are playing with an advantage. These teams are playing with an advantage that their competitors do not have and that’s not how sports work.”

Wiggins sat patiently next to Spokane-based attorney Andrew Wagley, later admitting to the nerves and anxiety he felt as Downton and Askew went back and forth with arguments.

“My heart was beating every second of it, but I just tried to stay positive,” he said. “Shout out to Ryan, he did an amazing job. That’s probably the most locked in I’ve been listening to anybody. You know at school, those teachers be talking, but I was very locked in like, we got this, we got this.”

After 50 minutes of arguments from both sides, Chuang called for a 15-minute intermission and handed down the injunction order shortly after the hearing resumed. Citing a shortage of judicial officers, Chuang couldn’t schedule trial until May 10, 2027, meaning Wiggins’ case wouldn’t be heard until one month after Gonzaga’s season ended, at the earliest. As part of the ruling, Chuang also restrained the NCAA from enforcing the rule of restitution, meaning the governing body won’t be able to retroactively strip Gonzaga of victories or postseason awards while Wiggins is on the court.

Wiggins broke into a smile when the hearing ended and quickly found his teammates, trading hugs with all six in attendance before the group exited the courtroom.

“Those are my brothers. I’m just happy they came and supported me,” Wiggins said. “I transferred here for a reason, to win, and it’s just showing that off-the-court chemistry we have.”

Even as eligibility restrictions prevented him competing against Purdue and New Mexico State, Wiggins was able to establish some semblance of chemistry on the court through practices since arriving in Spokane two months ago.

“I’m very excited,” Wiggins said. “I’ve been waiting for this opportunity ever since I knew I could come back to college, so I’m just ready to play Saturday and play for the rest of the year.”

What exactly are the Zags getting from the newly-eligible wing? An extremely-capable outside shooter, for one. Wiggins made 72 total 3-pointers last season at FSU - 24 more than anyone on Gonzaga’s roster - and connected at a 38.7% clip from behind the arc while averaging 13.3 points per game.

“Just expect everything, expect us to win and expect some of my 3-pointers because I know everybody’s looking for that,” Wiggins said.

The experienced wing is a proven winner who played on Clemson teams that combined to go 74-30 between 2022-25 before starring on a Florida State team that went 18-15 in coach Luke Loucks’ first season and declined an invitation to the NIT.

“I’m really just looking to play, just to win, show my skillset,” Wiggins said. “Really just win, stay positive and just having faith out there on the court. I’m just very glad I got this opportunity.”

Gonzaga.title: LSU beat writer discusses coach Will Wade, Tigers keys vs. Gonzaga | Q&A
Gonzaga.summary:
LSU’s roster construction was in the national spotlight during the offseason as the program waited on eligibility waivers, court rulings and NCAA clearance on international standouts.

The talented Tigers might remain in the spotlight during the season as a force in the SEC and beyond.

LSU has averaged 94 points per game with a 41.3-point margin of victory in blowouts over three overmatched opponents.

The Tigers, picked No. 14 in the 16-team SEC preseason poll, have climbed to No. 27 in KenPom’s rankings after starting out at 47. Gonzaga, which faces LSU on Saturday at the Spokane Arena, checks in at No. 11.

We connected with Toyloy Brown III, who covers LSU for the Advocate newspaper based in Baton Rouge, for a closer look at the Tigers.

Q: At one point in late September, LSU’s official roster listed just four players, but coach Will Wade remained optimistic throughout that the roster would eventually take shape.

Now that the roster is largely set, highlight a player or two that will be crucial to the Tigers’ season.

Brown: Donovan Dent is essential for LSU to reach its ceiling. The 6-foot-2 point guard epitomizes what it means to be a floor general with his elite court vision and creativity as a playmaker. He remains poised under heavy defensive pressure, posting a 25-to-3 assist-to-turnover ratio thus far.

Dent has been just as electric on defense as an ideal fit for the high-pressure defense LSU employs. He isn’t only averaging over three steals per game, but also leads the team with 2.3 blocks, an underrated trait from his time at his previous stops.

LSU 7-footer Michael Ruzic has been remarkable despite coming off the bench. The 20-year-old from Croatia came to college with a reputation as a tall shooter. He started his collegiate career with an added 15 pounds to his now 235-pound frame that has complemented his skill as a finisher.

He has made an incredible 29 of 30 shots in the paint. His rim protection without fouling and overall awareness have also been better than expected early.

Q: Guessing this isn’t the first or last time you’ll be asked this: What is it like covering LSU coach Will Wade as a beat writer?

Brown: A Wade press conference is never boring. It’s hard for me to imagine there being many more college coaches as unfiltered. He is almost too quotable. If I include all the fun things he says, all my stories would be 1,000 words. I also have to be ready to record video at a moment’s notice. You never know when he’ll joke that NIL stands for “now it’s legal.”

The only not-so-fun part of covering Wade was the mystery of who is or will be on the team and when or if they’ll be eligible. Only four rotation players were certain to play before the season opener. Other than that, it has been a fun ride.

Q: LSU has stomped three overmatched opponents to open the season. Your takeaways of the team’s strengths/weaknesses thus far?

Brown: LSU did what it was supposed to do: crush teams with inferior talent. It did so in historic fashion, winning three straight games by 40 or more points for the first time. Its latest 40-point win over Louisiana Tech was the most impressive since KenPom’s model predicted only a 22-point win.

One strength has been the defensive intensity. The full-court and half-court pressure Wade’s team is playing with has bothered opponents even more than anticipated. Players like Dent and starting small forward Saliou Niang are not just aggressive but cerebral disruptors on and off the ball.

One weakness has been 3-point shooting. LSU’s starting shooting guard Skyy Clark is 1 of 16 from beyond the arc. The sharpshooter is in a cold spell that the team isn’t worried about. However, besides backup two-guard Abdi Bashir, there aren’t other players who are reliably going to take, let alone make, multiple 3-pointers in a game.

While LSU can be an elite two-point scoring squad, it will be tough to win against strong opponents if Clark and Bashir are missing.

Q: What are a couple of keys for LSU to be successful against Gonzaga?

Brown: One key will be rebounding. LSU hasn’t dominated its lesser competition on the glass enough, specifically defensively. The Tigers have the size to do better, but they’re relying on French center Brice Dessert, who is still adjusting to the pace of the American game.

Giving second-chance scoring opportunities to players like Braden Huff will be much more harmful than it was against Louisiana Tech.

Another key will be the turnover margin. Gonzaga has been exceptional at securing the ball so far. If LSU has a similar number of field goal attempts, Mark Few’s team will win. LSU will use a full-court press to force live-ball turnovers that can grease the wheel of its offense.

Wade won’t expect to force 23 turnovers as it did against Louisiana Tech, so he’ll need his players to be sound decision-makers and value their possessions. Forfeiting easy looks to Gonzaga’s already high-powered offense is a death knell.

Gonzaga.title: Analyzing Gonzaga's 2-0 start, and a look ahead to LSU | Zags Basketball Insiders Podcast
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga has handled Purdue and New Mexico State, but the challenge figures to get tougher Saturday against LSU in the Spokane Veterans Memorial Arena.

Richard Fox and yours truly discussed what we’ve seen from No. 14 Gonzaga thus far and size up the showdown against the 3-0 Tigers in the latest Zags Insiders Podcast.

Find the entire podcast at spokesman.com/podcasts/zags-basketball-insiders/ or YouTube on The Spokesman-Review’s channel. Here are a few excerpts, edited for space considerations.

Early impressions

Fox: We talked about needing some time to understand what this group is. It’s pretty evident, and this is not a surprise because it’s Gonzaga basketball, they’re going to be very good offensively. The first couple games, averaging eight turnovers, assisting on something like 42% of their shots, assisting on makes.

The 3-point shot, 19 of 40, 48%. That’s a really small sample size and I still have PTSD from the last three seasons, but early returns indicate that we’re looking at a team that’s not going to be bad (on 3s).

They put a lot of foul pressure on teams and they’re getting out on the break. The offensive potential is as good as we’ve seen in quite a while.

On the flip side, the defense and rebounding have not been great. Purdue’s (7-foot-4 Daniel) Jacobsen, yes he’s big and they’re very fundamental, but they’re not a big team. New Mexico State doesn’t have high-major size, even though they have some guys that are good and crafty. Gonzaga is just plus-7 in two games on the glass.

Meehan: The best stat of that entire game (vs. NMSU) wasn’t the three players that had 20 points. I don’t even think it was (Xaivian) Lee’s 10 assists. He’s off to a great start. Davis Fogle’s six assists, I think, that’s a very important stat as much as his (22) points.

He’s truly a guy that can create and dish. He’s taking on a lot of the offensive load right now. They do have other guys that can create but he can really create. He can draw the big, he can draw the help from the wing and that maybe is creating some open looks that they’re cashing in on.

Isiah Harwell can shoot it when he is set and his form (is good). When he’s drifting or forcing it or rushing it, that’s a different story.

If Fogle can (create), that can really alleviate (pressure on others). They’ve got capable scorers.

Talking Tigers

Meehan: Somewhere in that top 10 or 15, LSU’s lineup would probably rank there for sure. The Zags will know a few of these guys, (former UCLA guards) Donovan Dent and Skyy Clark.

Dent had that great run at New Mexico and he came along last year (at UCLA) and put up good numbers. He’s legitimately a great college player. Clark is a very good shooter. He hasn’t found it yet (1 of 16 on 3-pointers), but he’s way better than that.

It’s going to be a battle physically. It’s going to be interesting how it is whistled. Massamba Diop has been in foul trouble pretty much every time he’s suited up. The Zags have been putting a lot of foul pressure on people. These are big, athletic kids, some 22- and 23-year old bodies going at it.

If you look at the offensive rebounding category after the game, you’re going to have a pretty good indication of who wins.

Fox: Gonzaga is going to have to rebound at a much higher level than they have to start the year.

LSU has a lot of talent. Just like GU, they have to get all these pieces together. Dent is a high-level guard. He can really control the game. LSU is going to want to play fast.

It’s going to be a real test for (Nathan) De Sousa, (Javon) Bennett, Lee and Gonzaga as a whole to try to corral him. LSU is one of the few teams in the country that I’d be nervous about trying to run with for 40 minutes. I think you want to force them to score over you.

Their European (players), that’s the hard part. You don’t have a lot of film, you don’t necessarily know who they are, even if you’re super dialed into the Euro game. This is going to be a legitimate test.

Gonzaga.title: With sights on Gonzaga-LSU matchup, Chauncey Wiggins has 5-in-5 eligibility hearing moved to Thursday
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga is running a hurry-up offense in its attempt to get Chauncey Wiggins on the court before Saturday’s marquee nonconference matchup with LSU at Numerica Veterans Arena.

The Florida State transfer is now set to appear at an injunction hearing at 1:30 p.m. Thursday before Superior Court Judge Dean Chuang. If granted, the injunction could allow Wiggins to make his Gonzaga debut against the Tigers.

Wiggins was not initially scheduled to have his 5-in-5 eligibility case heard until Nov. 17, eliminating the possibility that he’d suit up in Saturday’s game. Wiggins’ attorneys, Carl Oreskovich and Andrew Wagley of Spokane-based firm Etter, McMahon, Lamberson, Van Wert & Oreskovich, P.C., filed a motion to shorten time that was approved by Spokane Superior Court, bumping the injunction hearing up by five days.

In a motion to shorten time posted to the Spokane Superior Court web docket, Wiggins’ attorneys contest the player will continue to “suffer irreparable harm” with every game missed this season, “particularly primetime games in the national spotlight.” The motion also argued the NCAA will “suffer essentially no harm” if an injunction is granted.

Wiggins dressed in street clothes and didn’t play in both of Gonzaga’s wins last week – a 78-72 victory over Purdue in Las Vegas in the season opener and a 109-68 blowout of New Mexico State on Saturday at McCarthey Athletic Center.

A 6-foot-10 wing who averaged 13.3 points on 38% 3-point shooting last season at Florida State, Wiggins originally joined a group of student-athletes seeking a fifth season of eligibility through the Godfrey vs. NCAA 5-in-5 lawsuit filed in Wiggins’ home state of Georgia. The plaintiffs were successful, earning an injunction that cleared them to compete, but the case was ultimately stayed, reversing the verdict until oral arguments were heard on Jan. 12.

Seeking expedited relief, Wiggins and other plaintiffs refiled in Waco, Texas, joining student-athletes who’d previously received a temporary restraining order in the Wheeler vs. NCAA 5-in-5 case. A judge heard the case four days before Gonzaga’s opener against Purdue, but dismissed the TRO and denied the special appearance, citing “lack of personal jurisdiction.”

Wiggins’ eligibility fight continues in Spokane County, where Oreskovich will represent him. Last October, Oreskovich helped former Gonzaga player Tyon Grant-Foster secure an injunction that allowed Grant-Foster to play for Mark Few’s team in 2025-26. Chuang, who was appointed to the 13th judgeship by then-Gov. Jay Inslee in 2023, is a Walla Walla native who resided in Olympia before attending Gonzaga Law School.

Three declaration affidavits, from Wiggins, Few and Gonzaga Compliance Director Scott Garrison, were also filed to the Superior Court docket on Monday, as was a pro hac vice motion that allows Ryan Downton – Wiggins’ primary attorney in the Georgia and Texas lawsuits – to participate in the lawsuit.

Gonzaga’s coach argued “it is critically important for Mr. Wiggins that he be allowed to compete as soon as possible,” stressing that “each day he misses will postpone his ability to learn the system, mesh with teammates, and ultimately delay his ability to perform in competition games under a national spotlight.”

Gonzaga.summary: SAN RAMON, Calif. – In the first edition of the honor this season, Gonzaga's Davis Fogle was named the Pac-12 Offensive Player of the Week Monday.

Gonzaga.title: Unbeaten week moves Gonzaga up one spot to No. 14 in Associated Press poll
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga’s perfect start to the regular season came with a slight bump in Monday’s Associated Press Top 25 poll.

The Zags moved up one spot to No. 14 after narrowly beating Purdue 78-72 in the season opener at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas and cruising for a 109-68 home victory against New Mexico State.

There was no movement inside the top four of the first regular-season Top 25 poll, but 19 of the 21 teams ranked between No. 5 and No. 25 moved up or down at least one spot, with UCLA making the biggest jump of anyone, shooting up 13 spots to No. 9 after an 84-75 victory over former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd and Arizona in Vegas. The loss also dropped Arizona seven spots to No. 12 in the new poll.

The top 10 consists of No. 1 Florida, No. 2 Duke, No. 3 Illinois, No. 4 UConn, No. 5 Michigan State, No. 6 Virginia, No. 7 Texas, No. 8 Houston, No. 9 UCLA and No. 10 Louisville.

The Zags are positioned to play three top-10 teams – Duke, Michigan State and UCLA – during the nonconference schedule. Seven of Gonzaga’s potential opponents at the Players Era 16 also held down spots in Monday’s poll: No. 10 Louisville, No. 11 Tennessee, No. 13 St. John’s, No. 16 Texas Tech, No. 17 Miami, No. 18 Alabama and No. 20 Michigan.

Four other possible opponents in Vegas – Iowa State, Baylor, TCU and Creighton – another potential second-round opponent in Vegas, received Top 25 votes. The Zags will see Creighton later on, visiting the Bluejays for a Dec. 12 game in Omaha.

Utah State was the only other Pac-12 team to receive a Top 25 vote. The Aggies appeared on one ballot, at No. 25, after opening the season with comfortable wins over Idaho State and Omaha.

Gonzaga didn’t move in Monday’s USA Today Coaches Poll, remaining at No. 12.

Gonzaga.title: No. 15 Gonzaga Rolls Past New Mexico State, 109-68
Gonzaga.summary: SPOKANE, Wash. (AP) — Davis Fogle and Isiah Harwell each scored 22 points, Braden Huff added 20 and No. 15 Gonzaga beat New Mexico State 109-68 on Saturday.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's passing gets passing grade in blowout of New Mexico State | Rewind
Gonzaga.summary:
It could be the first of many reminders from Mark Few this season. Even Gonzaga can be vulnerable against an overmatched opponent when things like defense, rebounding and general effort are lagging.

The 15th-ranked Zags struggled in all three areas during the first half of Saturday’s home opener against New Mexico State, but a halftime message from Few kicked the hosts into gear, allowing them to pull away for a 109-68 victory at McCarthey Athletic Center.

“It was the effort and more dictating things instead of kind of sitting back and reacting,” Few said. “We talked about being proactive and I thought we were reactive through that first half and even for the first five, six minutes of the second half and we flipped a switch. When we do that, then we’ve got a chance.

“When it’s the other way, we’re putting ourselves in position where guys can make shots and make plays and get fouls on us and it’s hard to get separation when you’re like that.”

In today’s rewind, we look at the team’s impressive assist-to-turnover numbers against New Mexico State, how a former Gonzaga assistant pocketed a signature win on Friday and the walk-on guard who had an eventful college debut Saturday afternoon.

Quick and under control

Gonzaga had varying levels of success distributing the ball in two exhibition games and Monday’s season opener, dishing out 13 assists against Arkansas, 23 against NAIA Lewis-Clark State and 15 against Purdue.

It’s usually one of two primary statistical columns that dictates whether a team is successful moving the ball. The Zags had been stagnant in the other one, committing exactly 10 turnovers in each of their three previous games.

On Saturday, there was finally some movement in the turnover column – the right kind – for a team that hit on all cylinders offensively while eclipsing 100 points with 4 minutes, 19 seconds to play.

Gonzaga left the Kennel pleased with both numbers, delivering 23 assists while committing only six turnovers against an athletic New Mexico State that pressured the ball and occasionally picked up full court.

The Zags are trying to strike a fine line this season by pushing the tempo while valuing ball security and keeping turnover numbers at a minimum.

“I stressed that all summer and all fall,” Few said. “We’ve had such incredible offensive teams up here, but what kind of doesn’t get covered was how well those teams took care of the ball. That’s what made the Nembhards so special. They would routinely go 12 assists, one turnover or 10 assists, no turnovers. I think we all started taking it for granted.”

There’s no Nembhard on this roster, but there is a point guard who hails from the Toronto area and one who, ironically enough, made the same move Andrew Nembhard did by transferring from Florida to Gonzaga.

Fifth-year addition Xaivian Lee has been Gonzaga’s starting point guard through the exhibitions and both regular-season games. Lee has impressed despite a short runway to learn Gonzaga’s system and personnel after committing in late August. Four days after scoring 18 points against Purdue, Lee put on a passing clinic versus New Mexico State, totaling 10 assists and just one turnover in 28 minutes on the floor.

Lee and sophomore wing Davis Fogle combined for 16 assists with just one turnover. Nobody on Gonzaga’s roster had more than one turnover and two starters, Braden Huff and Massamba Diop, didn’t account for one.

“Hopefully this team’s starting to figure it out because we were a little bit turnover prone early,” Few said. “But it’s a huge key, to me it’s the key to being really efficient. That and shot selection on the offensive end.”

Purdue beaters

Few and Roger Powell have remained close since the former assistant left Gonzaga’s coaching staff four years ago to become the head coach at Valparaiso and it was almost a certainty the two would touch base at some point this week with a common opponent on their early nonconference schedules.

Four days after Few and Gonzaga squeaked out a 78-72 victory over Purdue in Las Vegas, Powell and Valparaiso visited the Boilermakers at Mackey Arena. Powell phoned Few at some point during the week to discuss strategy and inquire about anything that could help the Beacons in a game they entered as 19½-point underdogs.

It’s unclear to what extent Few’s advice helped, but it probably didn’t hurt as Valparaiso made one buzzer-beater at the end of the first overtime period and another in the second to claim a victory that could be in the running for the biggest upset of the 2026-27 college basketball season.

“Roger and I talk all the time and obviously we wanted to share stuff with Purdue,” Few said. “We were all watching it last night, the team watched it, or at least the last two minutes and the overtime.”

Valparaiso guard Rakim Chaney erupted for 35 points and knocked down a game-tying 3-pointer at the end of the first overtime period before fouling out. Backcourt mate Justus McNair delivered the second clutch shot of the night, sinking a buzzer-beating 3 from the left elbow to send Valpo home with the victory.

Few emphasized the importance of signature wins for midmajor teams looking to build momentum and gain respect on a national scale. Gonzaga’s coach would know better than most as someone who picked up a handful of those victories early on his Hall of Fame tenure in Spokane.

“When you’re at that point with your program, you’re making gains, making gains,” Few said. “But you need something like that to kind of show everybody you are making gains. He’s done a wonderful job there and he’s just an incredible human being. Everybody roots for Roger, man. He’s the best.”

Powell’s first Valparaiso team went just 7-25 in 2023-24, but the Beacons improved in the win column each season, going 15-19 in 2024-25 before finally securing a winning record in 2025-26 with an 18-15 finish. Valparaiso improved to 2-0 this season with Friday’s victory while Purdue dropped to 0-2 for the first time under 21st-year coach Matt Painter.

Chipped tooth

Even with Gonzaga’s lead at 38 points, walk-on guard Alonzo Metz brought hustle and physicality to the final 2 minutes, 21 seconds of Saturday’s blowout.

He has a chipped tooth to show for it as well.

Metz subbed in late and elevated for an offensive rebound 35 seconds into his college debut. After securing the board, the 5-foot-11 guard went back up for a jumper, catching an elbow to his mouth as he watched the ball ricochet off the rim.

Metz quickly noticed he’d lost a chunk of his middle tooth, recovered it on the hardwood and chucked it toward Gonzaga’s bench. The guard missed one more shot but added another offensive rebound to his personal tally before the final buzzer sounded.

Gonzaga teammates reacted to the sequence during postgame interviews.

“It was pretty cool,” Fogle said. “That sucks to happen, but he kept playing. Might look a little funky right now, but he’ll be back.”

“That fired us up,” Braden Huff said. “I mean it sucks, you’re in there for two minutes and you lose your tooth but he’s a fighter. He got two rebounds in those two minutes and made a bunch of small plays, so excited for him and not necessarily excited for that tooth but he’ll be all right.”

“Me personally, I love it,” Isiah Harwell said. “I love it, I love it.”

Gonzaga.title: Allie Turner, Lauren Whittaker help Gonzaga get back on track with win over UC Riverside 85-58
Gonzaga.summary:
Course correction made.

Now that doesn’t mean that everything with the Gonzaga women’s basketball team is peachy and without flaw. But 44 hours after what they called an embarrassing loss, the Bulldogs had their best start of the season.

Call the Zags’ 85-58 win over the UC Riverside Highlanders on Sunday before 4,521 at McCarthey Athletic Center a step in the right direction.

For the first time in three games, Gonzaga scored the first basket. And the cold-shooting Highlanders contributed as well, missing their first 16 shots from the field. A basket from forward Lauren Whittaker capped a 14-1 start.

The Bulldogs (2-1) never led in the loss to Idaho on Friday. They never trailed against UCR (1-2).

“We had a lot better energy,” GU coach Lisa Fortier said. “We rebounded a heckuva lot better. I liked the pace better. It’s nice to be the team that sets the tone versus the team that’s having to respond.”

Gonzaga’s starting forwards, Whittaker and Taylor Smith, said the correction started in an early practice Saturday.

“We just took the rest of the day (Friday, after the loss) to get all of our emotions out,” said Smith, who was one of four Zags in double-figure scoring with 12 points, seven rebounds, four assists and two steals. “We talk a lot about the process. So just moving on and bringing good energy to practice … we had a really good practice and prepared well for (Sunday). We started off well and it went from there.”

Whittaker had her second double-double with 14 points and 14 rebounds to go with five assists and four steals.

“Knowing that the last two games were a bit rough to start, we knew we had to come out and punch first,” Whittaker said. “Even just simplifying everything to just getting the first bucket. Taking baby steps like that. The team rallied after the Idaho loss.”

Guard Allie Turner, who didn’t take a shot in the first quarter, matched Whittaker’s 14 points and Teryn Gardner, who came off the bench after starting the first two games, had 11 with five steals.

Gardner hit a 3-pointer off a pass from Whittaker to give Gonzaga its biggest first-half lead at 28-12 with 4:20 to go in the second quarter.

Gonzaga’s lead never got below double digits.

Another Gardner 3-pointer late in the third extended the Bulldogs’ lead to 55-35.

A third Gardner 3-pointer put the Zags ahead by their largest margin at 78-51 with 2:31 remaining.

Gonzaga was outrebounded by smaller Idaho on Friday. Sunday the Zags won the boards 49-30.

They also had 17 steals, forcing most of UCR’s 22 turnovers.

“Defense has to continue to be a focus for us,” Fortier said. “There’s good offensive players who are gonna try to exploit us.”

Fortier saw a number of positives and things her team will learn.

“We need to learn from all the games,” she said. “There’s plenty to learn from this game, but I think we responded really well. The team seemed focused (at practice) and they came out looking like it today. So often it’s how you start.”

Now Gonzaga hits the road for the first time with stops at Grand Canyon on Friday and Stanford on Sunday before returning home Nov. 18 against Montana.

“It’s a hard road trip,” Fortier said. “I’ve never been to Grand Canyon before, but I’ve seen the pictures and videos. They get a lot of support and they run a difficult style that was hard for us last year. That’s going to be one thing. And then you go to Stanford and it’s a very different game and they have a different team than they had last year. They’re always extremely skilled, very disciplined, they execute really well and they’re really smart. Two tough places to play and a good chance for us to test ourselves.”

Gonzaga.title: Trio of 20-point scorers lifts Gonzaga to 109-68 victory over New Mexico State in home opener
Gonzaga.summary:
The defense went through lulls in the first and second half. The physicality wasn’t always up to par. The rebounding came and went before ultimately turning into a net positive for 15th-ranked Gonzaga.

None of it may have mattered in the end for a Gonzaga team that had three 20-point scorers and five double-digit scorers in a 109-68 thumping of New Mexico State in Saturday’s home opener at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Even with inconsistent play in other areas, Gonzaga could usually toss the ball to Isiah Harwell, Davis Fogle or Braden Huff and expect good things to happen on a night that saw the trio combine for 64 points, 25 field goals and seven 3-pointers.

Harwell, Fogle and Huff kept the Zags afloat offensively until the defense came around in the second half, allowing Gonzaga to create separation and reach the century mark for the first time since Mark Few’s team hung 109 points on North Florida in a nonconference game last season.

Harwell registered 22 points on a career-high scoring night for the Houston transfer, who reached 20 points just one time last season against Jackson State. The guard finished 8 of 10 from the field, 4 of 6 from the 3-point line and 2 of 4 from the free throw line. Harwell, who had multiple steal-and-score sequences to spur GU’s transition offense, also led the Zags with three steals and added five rebounds.

“It feels blessed,” Harwell said. “Just being able to go out there and play the game I love again and have fun with it, it’s amazing.”

“He was hooping,” Fogle said of Harwell. “That’s his game, I expect a lot more of that. He can shoot it, he can score at all three levels and he’s just been such an anchor for us on the defensive side too. Then just doing all the little stuff. Rebounding, diving on the floor. So the scoring is just a plus.”

“Yeah, we’ve seen that all fall,” Huff added. “It’s good he was able to showcase that today. Like Davis said, expect a lot more of that this year.”

With 16 points in the first half, Fogle was on track to set a new career high for the second time this week after pacing Gonzaga with 22 points in Monday’s season opener against Purdue. The sophomore wing matched but failed to exceed Monday’s number, hitting 22 points in 33 minutes before being pulled from the game with five minutes, 41 seconds remaining in the second half. He finished 8 of 13 from the field, 3 of 6 from 3 and 3 of 4 from the stripe and contributed six assists.

Huff rebounded from an inefficient outing against Purdue, adding 20 points on 9 of 13 shooting.

Florida transfer Xaivian Lee set the table for Gonzaga’s trio of 20-point scorers, dishing out 10 assists – the point guard’s highest total since a Feb. 21 SEC game against Ole Miss last season. Lee and Fogle combined for 16 assists with just one turnover on a day that saw the Zags commit six as a team.

Gonzaga easily covered the 26½-point pregame spread despite a troubling first half. New Mexico State led for less than two minutes during the game’s opening stretch, but the Aggies controlled a few key statistical categories – namely rebounding and paint points – and went into halftime trailing by only five points.

Few’s message at halftime? Defense, defense and more defense.

“He just told us we had to toughen up,” Huff said. “I think that was the bottom line. Before he even came in, I think we all knew that. We reiterated that, so we just kind of had to hunker down, stick to the game plan and just ultimately toughen up. I think we did a much better job in the second half.”

Substantially better. Gonzaga outscored NMSU by a 62-26 point margin and went on a 22-2 scoring run that stretched the lead to 33 points with five minutes, 15 seconds to play.

Gonzaga’s improved outside shooting was on display in a game that saw the Bulldogs finish 13 of 24 (54%) from the 3-point line. The Aggies were limited to six made field goals and 28% shooting in the second half.

Javon Bennett contributed with 13 points off the bench while Massamba Diop had 12 points and seven rebounds, playing 33 minutes in a game where reserve forward Izan Almansa was sidelined with a calf injury.

Gonzaga (2-0) now shifts its attention to another marquee nonconference test, facing LSU (2-0) at 12:30 p.m. on Saturday at Numerica Veterans Arena. The game will air on USA Network.

Gonzaga.title: Isiah Harwell sets career-high in No. 15 Gonzaga's rout of New Mexico State 109-68
Gonzaga.summary:
Isiah Harwell set a new career-high with 22 points and No. 15 Gonzaga overcame shaky stretches in both halves to pull away from visiting New Mexico State for a 109-68 victory at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Gonzaga didn’t control the battle down low the way it normally does and went through defensive lulls in both the first and second half, but the Bulldogs still found enough production on the offensive end from Harwell, Davis Fogle and Braden Huff, who all had at least 20 points and combined for 64 in Saturday’s home opener.

Harwell beat his previous career-high of 20 points, set last season with Houston in a game against New Mexico State, and finished 8 of 10 from the field, 4 of 6 from the 3-point line and 2 of 4 from the free throw line. Harwell also led the Zags with three steals and pulled down five rebounds.

Fogle matched the career-high he set four days earlier against Purdue, scoring 22 points on 8 of 13 from the field, 3 of 6 from 3 and 3 of 4 from the stripe. Huff rebounded from an inefficient outing against Purdue, adding 20 points on 9 of 13 shooting.

Florida transfer Xaivian Lee set the table for Gonzaga’s trio of 20-point scorers, dishing out 10 assists – the point guard’s highest total since a Feb. 21 SEC game against Ole Miss last season.

Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop was effective in his 33 minutes, registering 12 points and seven rebounds, while Dayton transfer Javon Bennett gave Gonzaga another 13 points off the bench, finishing 2 of 3 from the 3-point line.

There were plenty of open looks for Gonzaga from the 3-point line in a game that saw Mark Few’s team finish 13 of 24 from deep.

After leading by just five points at halftime, the Zags outscored the Aggies 62-26 after the break.

Gonzaga (2-0) will now shift its attention to another marquee nonconference test, facing LSU (2-0) at 12:30 p.m. on Saturday at Numerica Veterans Arena. The game will air on USA Network.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Izan Almansa sidelined for New Mexico State game with lower leg injury
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga won’t be able to rely on Izan Almansa’s steady bench production in today’s home opener against New Mexico State.

The sophomore forward isn’t available against the Aggies as he recovers from a lower right leg injury, according to Gonzaga. Almansa is listed as day to day, but didn’t appear to be in any real discomfort walking around the court in street clothes before tipoff at McCarthey Athletic Center.

After Saturday’s game, the Zags don’t play again until Nov. 14 against LSU at Numerica Veterans Arena. They have one more game, on Nov. 17 at home against Montana State, before traveling to Las Vegas for the Players Era Festival.

Almansa provided instant offense and rebounding off the bench in Gonzaga’s exhibition games and Monday’s season-opening win against Purdue.

The Spanish forward spelled starting center Massamba Diop when the Arizona State encountered first-half foul trouble and supplied 11 points on 4 of 6 shooting to go with four rebounds in 29 minutes off the bench.

Almansa was effective in a preseason exhibition against Arkansas one day after learning the NCAA approved his eligibility waiver, scoring 14 points and pulling down six rebounds in 29 bench minutes. He registered another 12 points on 4 of 5 shooting in a blowout exhibition win over NAIA Lewis-Clark State.

With Almansa sidelined, sophomore forward Parker Jefferson or freshman center Sam Funches likely become Gonzaga’s first big off the bench. Neither saw playing time in Monday’s opener against Purdue.

Outside of Almansa, fifth-year senior wing Chauncey Wiggins was the only other Gonzaga player who didn’t suit up on Saturday. Wiggins is still in eligibility limbo and likely won’t learn whether he’ll be able to suit up for the Zags until a Nov. 17 injunction hearing at Spokane Superior Court.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga’s small-ball lineup yields mixed results during home opener
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga turned to a small-ball lineup at times Saturday against New Mexico State with Izan Almansa sitting out with a sore calf.

The results: Some good, some bad at both ends of the floor.

Almansa has been solid as the first big off the bench behind starters Braden Huff and Massamba Diop in exhibition games and the season-opening win over Purdue last Monday.

“He banged his calf,” coach Mark Few said of the 6-foot-10 junior forward from Spain. “It’s just been slow to respond. He’ll be fine.”

Gonzaga shifted sophomores Isiah Harwell or Davis Fogle to the ‘4’ position in the first half when Huff needed a breather. Those two saw time at the 4 in the second half when Diop picked up his third and fourth fouls near the 10-minute mark and spent time on bench.

Huff checked out for good with 7:28 remaining in Gonzaga’s 109-68 blowout victory at McCarthey Athletic Center.

The 6-6, 216-pound Harwell lined up against 6-8 Mark Lavrenov and Fogle took some reps on the Aggies forward. NMSU fed Lavrenov repeatedly late in the first half and he responded with power moves and buckets against Harwell and Fogle and a pair of free throws after drawing a foul on Diop.

Lavrenov had 12 points as New Mexico State trailed 47-42 after an offensive-minded first half.

“No, that was my first time,” Harwell said of defending a 4. “Hope Izan can come back though because boxing out those 4s can be a little struggle. It was good though.”

The trade-offs certainly worked both ways. Lavrenov scored a team-high 19 points but he and his teammates had all kinds of issues matching up defensively against Huff, Fogle and Harwell.

The Zag trio combined for 64 points on 25 of 36 shooting. GU also won the rebounding 30-26 and paint points 42-34. Harwell actually outrebounded Lavrenov 5-4 and Fogle pulled down four boards to go with six assists. Diop added 12 points and seven rebounds.

“We miss Izan, he’s kind of a jack of all trades,” Few said. “He does a lot, especially in a game like that. He reminds me of Killian (Tillie) and Anton (Watson) a little bit. They had a really good 4-man. They did a great job of isolating him and taking advantage, especially when we went small, so we had to bring double teams.

“In the second half, we did a better job of getting our switches down and just being a tougher team.”

Indeed, the Zags outscored NMSU 62-26 in the final 20 minutes. The Aggies’ shooting percentage plummeted from 55.6% in the opening half to 28.6% in the second.

“I kind of did it a little bit last year,” Fogle said of guarding 4s. “On offense, just tried to space and use our speed against the bigs. On defense, make sure we box out, hit someone and just be tougher on the defensive side when playing small.”

Gonzaga.title: Davis Fogle fills up points, assists columns in rout | 3 takeaways
Gonzaga.summary:
Three takeaways at the buzzer from No. 15 Gonzaga’s 109-68 win over New Mexico State on Saturday at the McCarthey Athletic Center.

Dishin’ Davis

Gonzaga sophomore Davis Fogle is obviously a gifted scorer.

But Saturday, he also put his scoring and play-making ability on display.

The 6-foot-7 forward has pocketed 22 points in each of GU’s first two wins to open the season. As impressive as his 8-of-13 shooting, including 3 of 6 on 3s, was against the Aggies, it was another stat column that was equally important to the Zags.

Fogle handed out six assists, matching the career high he set as a freshman against Portland and in the West Coast Conference Tournament against Santa Clara last season.

Fogle’s driving ability often drew an extra defender and he capitalized by finding open teammates. In one first-half sequence, he hit a 3-pointer after a pass from Xaivian Lee, fed Lee for a 3-ball and then dunked home a lob pass from Lee.

Fogle has just two turnovers in two games.

Bennett takes advantage of added playing time

Senior guard Javon Bennett saw extended minutes with forward Izan Almansa sidelined by a calf strain and reserve point guard Nathan De Sousa whistled for three fouls in just three first-half minutes.

Bennett, a transfer guard from Dayton, had a nice stretch after checking in with roughly 5 minutes remaining in the first half. He hit a jumper in the lane and hit one of two free throws after drawing a foul on a drive into the paint.

Bennett followed with a 3-pointer and a pull-up jumper to help rebuild Gonzaga’s halftime lead to 47-42 after the Aggies had closed within two points.

Bennett finished with 13 points, hitting 4 of 6 shots, in just 19 minutes. He also had two steals.

He had five points, including a pair of free throws with 19 seconds left to boost GU’s lead to 76-71 over Purdue in the season opener.

Home sweet home

Gonzaga’s 78-72 win over Purdue last Monday pushed its winning streak to 23 straight in season openers, dating back to a loss to Saint Joseph’s in 2003 at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

The Zags’ streak in home openers is now at 38 after GU pulled away from New Mexico State in the second half. The Aggies were within two late in the first half and made it interesting at times, but they only led for 1 minute, 34 seconds.

The last time Gonzaga lost a home opener? Boise State edged GU 73-65 in 1988-89 at the Martin Centre.

Gonzaga.title: Days after losing to Gonzaga, Purdue stunned in 2OT by Valparaiso, former GU assistant coach
Gonzaga.summary:
WEST LAFAYETTE, Ind. – The Purdue Boilermakers are off to their worst start in 50 years.

After losing to No. 15 Gonzaga 78-72 on Monday in Las Vegas, Purdue returned home and expected to get back on track against an in-state mid-major opponent.

Valparaiso had other plans.

Led by fourth-year coach Roger Powell, who was an assistant at Gonzaga from 2019-23, Valparaiso knocked off Purdue 83-80 in double overtime at Mackey Arena. Purdue was a 19½-point favorite and lost to a Missouri Valley Conference opponent at home for the first time since Larry Bird played at Indiana State. It’s also Purdue’s first 0-2 start since 1976.

The Beacons (2-0) trailed by as many as 16 in the first half and were down 32-20 at halftime. They chipped away steadily in the second half and took their first lead with 4 minute, 49 seconds to go.

Justus McNair’s pullup jumper with 1:03 left in regulation was enough to send the game to overtime. There, leading scorer Rakim Chaney hit a wild shot at the buzzer to force another period.

Chaney was attempting a free throw with 4 seconds left and missed intentionally, letting the ball bounce three times high off the rim. Chaney was able to grab the rebound off a tip and spotted up for a 3-pointer, which he hit in the face of tight defense.

McNair came through in the second overtime, hitting a 25-foot 3-pointer at the buzzer for the win.

Chaney led with 35 points, while McNair added 17.

Much like Monday’s loss to Gonzaga, Purdue struggled to find its shot from outside, hitting 5 of 28 3-point attempts. Daniel Jacobsen led the Boilermakers with 28 points and 10 rebounds.

Powell’s team has improved in each of his four seasons at Valparaiso, going from 7-25 to 15-19 and 18-15 last season. The Beacons were picked fifth in the MVC preseason poll.

Powell, who played at Illinois from 2001-05, was interviewed by his former coach Bruce Weber after the game, who is now a commentator with Big Ten Network.

“You weren’t ready to be a head coach before, but you are tonight,” Weber said.

“I’m learning, I’m growing,” Powell said. “These guys are special. We’ve got a special bunch. … they never give up, that’s a part of our program, our culture we talk about grit and they showed a bunch of grit today.”

Gonzaga.title: New Mexico State has proven production, experience in shifty guard DJ Dudley | Key matchup
Gonzaga.summary:
New Mexico State had a good pulse on DJ Dudley before the Aggies visited Louisiana Tech last season for a Conference USA matchup on Feb. 4.

New Mexico State coach Jason Hooten watched film of the four games Dudley played before he squared off with the Aggies: a 25-point effort against Jacksonville State, 20-point efforts against Kennesaw State and UTEP and a 21-point game against Sam Houston State.

Those performances moved Dudley to the top of New Mexico State’s scouting report – if he wasn’t already there – and potentially put him near the top of Hooten’s offseason wish list. Dudley entered the transfer portal a few months later and committed to the Aggies on April 23, giving the fourth-year coach experience and production in his reconstructed backcourt.

Dudley is no longer on Hooten’s scouting report, but he’ll be at the top of opposing ones this season, including the scouting report No. 15 Gonzaga (1-0) is finalizing before Saturday’s 2 p.m. (KHQ) home opener against New Mexico State (1-0) at McCarthey Athletic Center.

“We took him because he was an all-conference guy who averaged 15 (points), helped his team go to the conference championship game,” Hooten said during a phone interview earlier this week. “He’s got that experience, he’s kind of been there and done that. Just really my biggest thing with him is taking that next step and having that level of consistency to where you can depend on him to be a guy you can ride a little bit.”

Dudley was an All-Conference USA First Team selection in 2025-26 and not surprisingly appeared on the 10-player Preseason All-Conference USA Team released last month.

A 6-foot-3 guard, Dudley averaged 13.8 points, 2.8 rebounds and 2.0 assists last season, shooting 43.1% from the field while making 36.2% from the 3-point line on 4.8 attempts per game. He averaged 14.8 ppg in C-USA games, reaching the 20-point threshold seven times in league play.

“Definitely a shot-maker, a guy that can play one on one and get a basket maybe when you need one,” Hooten said. “Trying to get him better and every coach is different. You play for a different coach, different style, different expectations. So he’s trying to learn those things. Good player and we’re going to have to have him now even more with Gabe out for the year.”

A native of Okinawa, Japan, Dudley is well-traveled. After playing high school basketball at LA (Los Angeles) Premier Prep, he started his college career at New Jersey-based Rider University in 2023-24 before transferring to Hutchinson Community College in Kansas and then Louisiana Tech.

Dudley’s junior season didn’t end on a good note – the guard had just five points on 2 of 16 shooting in a Conference USA title game loss to the Kennesaw State team Gonzaga faced in the opening round of the NCAA Tournament – but he’s off to a strong start at NMSU, scoring 22 points in Tuesday’s opener against Western New Mexico.

Dudley should be a good early-season test for Gonzaga’s Isiah Harwell, a quality perimeter defender who’s expected to take on most of the team’s top defensive assignments after spending a year with Kelvin Sampson at Houston.

Gonzaga.title: Compromised New Mexico State team grateful for Gonzaga opportunity: 'It's really hard to get these games anymore'
Gonzaga.summary:
Jason Hooten still sends out feelers during the offseason, but most of his phone calls to high-major programs soliciting interest in a nonconference game with New Mexico State culminate with the same response.

More often than not, something along the lines of “thanks, but no thanks.”

“It’s really, really hard to get these games anymore,” the Aggies’ fourth-year coach said earlier this week ahead of Saturday’s 2 p.m. (KHQ) meeting between No. 15 Gonzaga (1-0) and New Mexico State (1-0) at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Looking to turn a profit for their athletic department and capitalize on the few opportunities that exist to raise revenue-sharing dollars, New Mexico State and other midmajor programs are still incentivized to schedule so-called “buy games.”

The dilemma Hooten and coaching peers have encountered in recent years? Teams in the Big Ten, SEC, Big 12, ACC and Big East have become much less inclined to schedule them.

The NCAA’s NET rating, a tool used to sort and select the NCAA Tournament field, generally doesn’t reward high-major programs for blowout victories over capable midmajor opponents, but a narrow win or loss could damage the resume in a significant way. It’s better to play it safe and schedule teams projected to fall between 200-350 in the NET than those in the 100-200 range.

Since Hooten took over at New Mexico State in 2023-24, the Aggies have played three high-major opponents in total. Last season, they failed to get one on the schedule. So New Mexico State’s coach was equally surprised and relieved when Gonzaga agreed to squeeze the Aggies in, setting up just the second meeting between the schools.

“We were at a point in time where we needed a game like this financially,” Hooten said. “… I want to thank those guys for playing us, because it’s been really hard for us over the last two years since things have changed with the NET, it’s hard for these high majors to schedule good mid majors anymore.

“So it was awesome on their part to want to do this, because it was something we really needed. On the flip side, obviously a tough challenge for us. It’s a game that will definitely improve your team and these are the kind of games where if you don’t already know what to work on and improve on, you definitely will after a game like this probably.”

Gonzaga will see at least 10 high-major opponents in nonconference play, but outside of those higher-profile tests, Saturday’s game against New Mexico State could be the most challenging. The NET ratings aren’t out yet but the Aggies currently sit No. 131 at KenPom, slightly better than Montana State (No. 132) and significantly higher than Cornell (No. 205), Incarnate Word (No. 324) and NAIA Eastern Oregon teams visiting the Kennel over the next two months.

Picked to finish sixth in the preseason Conference USA poll, New Mexico State is also somewhat compromised coming out of a closer-than-expected 73-66 season-opening victory over Division II Western New Mexico on Tuesday.

The Aggies lost senior guard Gabe Warren, the team’s most consistent player during preseason practices and scrimmages, to a season-ending ACL injury after just nine minutes, and navigated the opener with seventh-year senior guard KK Robinson on a minutes restriction.

Robinson, who played two seasons at Arkansas, one at Texas A&M and one at Arkansas-Little Rock before missing consecutive seasons with double ACL injuries, is still working up to full speed and will be limited on Saturday against Gonzaga.

“We have so much to work on and improve on,” Hooten said. “I knew it was going to be a tough game (against Western New Mexico), just because in our scrimmages we had a little bit of everything but still we just hadn’t had our whole team together,” Hooten said. “So you’re trying to mix and match offense and you’re trying to mix and match positions. It’s kind of been wild and bizarre.”

Hooten, who spent 13 seasons coaching Sam Houston State, has a relationship with Gonzaga assistant Stephen Gentry, who previously worked under former Stephen F. Austin coach Brad Underwood in the Southland Conference.

“They’re tall and big and just really, really skilled,” Hooten said of Gonzaga. “I think coach Few has always done that. He’s always done a good job of recruiting really talented and skilled players, because they play the game the right way and they’re probably always one of the top offensive teams in the country.”

It will be a big task for New Mexico State’s starting frontcourt, 6-8 forward Mark Lavrenov and 6-9 forward Leopold Levillain, who’s operating at the ‘5’ spot for the Aggies this season. Levillain is a transfer from Long Beach State who previously played for the U-21 team at Cholet Basket in France. Gonzaga guard Nathan De Sousa had extensive experience with Cholet’s youth and senior teams before making the transition to college basketball.

Lavrenov averaged 9.9 points and 7.0 rebounds last season at Sacramento State and posted a double-double of 17 points and 10 rebounds against Western New Mexico. Lavrenov will likely match up with Gonzaga’s Braden Huff, who could be looking for a bounce-back game after finishing just 4 of 11 from the field in Monday’s opener against Purdue.

“It will be a great challenge for Mark to get to play against great size and length,” Hooten said. “Guys that are very established on that level. I know Mark though. Mark’s a tough kid and he plays really, really hard and passionate. I know he’ll be ready enough for the challenge.”

Gonzaga.title: Idaho women hold on for shocking upset over Gonzaga: 'It's a big win for us'
Gonzaga.summary:
The Idaho women’s basketball team stunned Gonzaga early and never relented Friday.

In a matchup of NCAA Tournament qualifiers from a year ago, the Vandals outplayed the Bulldogs in every facet, shocking the Zags 86-75 before 4,939 at McCarthey Athletic Center.

“If we could play every game like that it would be great,” Idaho coach Arthur Moreira said. “It’s like I told the girls, it’s a big win for us.”

Judging by his players reaction after the final buzzer, they celebrated like they won an NCAA Tournament game. And they had every reason to do so.

Still, it’s tough to discern what was most appalling about Gonzaga’s play, especially its start.

Junior guard Allie Turner summed it up as “embarrassing.”

Seven turnovers in the first 4 minutes or the fact Idaho had opened a 16-0 lead. Or that the Bulldogs allowed 54 points in the first half.

This summary can’t go any further without pointing out which team was the aggressor – and simply the best team – from the get go.

It must also be pointed out that Gonzaga was mediocre at best.

Before Gonzaga had got the license number of that truck from Moscow that ran it over early, the Vandals had opened a 16-0 lead.

It did get better for Gonzaga before things turned gross again for the Zags.

Zeryhia Aokuso hit a 3-pointer to pull Gonzaga within 27-20 with 8:39 to go before halftime. That’s as close as the Zags would get in the first half.

Idaho followed with back-to-back 3s, extending the lead to 33-20.

And the Vandals were only getting started. A 16-7 surge allowed Idaho to lead 54-34 when freshman guard Jacey Boesel of Deer Park got a steal and a layup in the waning seconds.

As it turned out, Gonzaga, which never had a lead, couldn’t get any closer than seven in the second half.

“We had our starting forwards on the bench (early) with two fouls. (And) in that part of the game we were turning it over,” Gonzaga coach Lisa Fortier said. “We didn’t force them to their weak hand at all. We offered very little defensive resistance. So I think it was a lot of things. We were getting our butts kicked on the glass from the start. So what is there to explain.”

Good point. It’s out of character for a Fortier-coached team to allow 54 points in an opening half, let alone 86 for the game.

Two Vandals nearly accounted for 60 of those points. Hope Hassmann and Ana Pinheiro scored 28 and 26 points respectively.

“It was a lot about our energy and effort on the court,” said Turner, who scored her 1,000th career point with a team-high 23. “They simply played harder than us and outcompeted us. That was the main message in the locker room. We just need to play harder, need to practice harder, we need to push each other more. That was pretty embarrassing. That’s good motivation for the future, but I wish it didn’t happen.”

Idaho (2-0) outrebounded the taller Zags 52-33. Gonzaga had 11 turnovers in the first half, but just one in the final two quarters.

The Vandals’ biggest lead came at 71-47 early in the fourth quarter. Idaho saw a 23-point lead to start the final period get trimmed to seven three times. But Idaho made 11 of 14 free throws in the final 1:17 to hold off GU.

“Just the little things – like not remembering stuff, not talking to each other,” said GU forward Taylor Smith, who had 12 points and five rebounds.

Idaho defended GU forward Lauren Whittaker well. She had just five points going into the fourth before finishing with 14 and seven rebounds.

“We had a unique game plan for Whittaker,” Moreira said. “It worked …. So we had to go away from it in the second half.”

Moreira said outrebounding teams is the standard for his team – win or lose.

“I know we’re not always the most talented, I know we don’t have the most resources, but we’re gonna recruit tough kids,” Moreira said. “And they’re gonna play hard … and they’re gonna rebound hard.”

Gonzaga (1-1) finishes a three-game homestand to open the season Sunday when UC Riverside visits. Tipoff is at 2 p.m.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Chauncey Wiggins takes third shot at eligibility, files new lawsuit in Spokane Superior Court
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga’s Chauncey Wiggins continues to exhaust every option in an ongoing attempt to secure a fifth season of eligibility.

After unsuccessful efforts in his home state of Georgia and in Texas, the transfer wing will now look for a favorable ruling in a legal jurisdiction significantly closer to Gonzaga’s campus, refiling in Spokane Superior Court on Thursday.

Wiggins, who filed an individual lawsuit against the NCAA after previously appearing in group 5-in-5 suits, is scheduled to have his case heard at 9 a.m. on Nov. 17 at the Spokane County Courthouse.

The player will be represented by Spokane-based attorneys Carl Oreskovich and Andrew Wagley, of Etter, McMahon, Lamberson, Van Wert and Oreskovich, P.C. Oreskovich worked with Tyon Grant-Foster last October to help the former Gonzaga wing secure an additional year of eligibility through an injunction in Spokane Superior Court.

Oreskovich and Wagley did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Spokesman-Review on Thursday night.

The date of Wiggins’ hearing isn’t optimal for Gonzaga and effectively keeps the wing out of at least two more games. The Zags host New Mexico State on Saturday before playing LSU in a high-profile nonconference game at Numerica Veterans Arena on Nov. 14.

In theory, Wiggins could secure a preliminary injunction or temporary restraining order on Nov. 17 and make his Gonzaga debut later the same night when Mark Few’s team hosts Montana State. Gonzaga fans might recall Grant-Foster securing an injunction last season and driving immediately to McCarthey Athletic Center to play in the team’s preseason exhibition against Eastern Oregon.

Wiggins continues to navigate the tricky 5-in-5 eligibility waters at a time when dozens of other fifth-year college basketball players around the country are suiting up and playing in regular-season games.

The 6-foot-10 wing from Atlanta initially joined the Godfrey v. NCAA lawsuit in Georgia, earning an injunction that cleared him to compete for Gonzaga. The NCAA filed for a stay motion, subsequently reversing the original ruling and making Wiggins ineligible until the case went to trial. With oral arguments not scheduled until mid-January, Wiggins withdrew from Godfrey v. NCAA and joined the Wheeler v. NCAA 5-in-5 lawsuit – along with other player plaintiffs from Georgia and Tennessee – in Waco, Texas.

A judge in McLennan County, Texas, dismissed Wiggins and other player plaintiffs from the case earlier this week, citing “lack of personal jurisdiction.”

Wiggins is now taking his third shot in Spokane Superior Court. The former Florida State and Clemson player sat out of Gonzaga’s season opener against Purdue while teammates Xaivian Lee and Javon Bennett – both of whom successfully sought eligibility relief in 5-in-5 lawsuits – contributed to the team’s 78-72 victory.

Should he become eligible, Wiggins would be a major asset for Gonzaga after making 157 career 3-pointers at his past two stops in the ACC and averaging 13.3 points last season for Florida State. Wiggins made 38.7% of his 3-pointers in 2025-26 and scored a career-high 31 points in a March 7 win over SMU.

Gonzaga.title: Revisiting the best moments, opponents and closest calls from Gonzaga's 23-year streak of season-opening wins
Gonzaga.summary:
A little bit of trivia for the loyal Gonzaga basketball historians out there: Which program great was making his college debut the last time Mark Few’s team dropped a season opener?

It’s a semi-challenging question, but one that becomes more simple and straightforward once you know the date, opponent and location. In 2003-04, Gonzaga made a cross-country trip to New York City and Madison Square Garden. There the Bulldogs squared off with legendary coach Phil Martelli and Saint Joseph’s in the Coaches vs. Cancer game.

The wiry freshman wing in Few’s starting lineup that night? Adam Morrison, who’d score 10 points on 5 of 10 shooting and added five rebounds in 31 minutes. Morrison helped Gonzaga secure a 38-34 halftime lead, but a loaded Saint Joseph’s roster featuring first-round NBA draft picks Jameer Nelson and Delonte West took control in the second half and the Hawks outscored the Bulldogs by 11 after the break to win 73-66.

The Hawks won 27 straight games, absorbed their first loss in the Atlantic 10 Tournament and advanced to the Elite Eight.

The Zags didn’t lose another opener, extending their streak to 23 straight years on Monday with a 78-72 victory over Purdue in Las Vegas.

Generally speaking, the Zags and other programs at their level adhere to similar scheduling strategies, opening against overmatched mid-majors. In Few’s first 21 seasons, the Zags played just two high-majors on opening night – Illinois in 2001 and Saint Joe’s in 2003 – but the coach has shifted his philosophy in recent years.

Three of GU’s last seven openers have been against teams from Power Five conferences, including Monday’s matchup with Purdue, a top Big Ten contender under Matt Painter.

“This is what these guys want to play,” Few told TNT sideline reporter Allie LaForce in a postgame interview. “At this point in my career, these are the games I’d like to play, so what the heck.”

With victory No. 23 now in hand, we decided to look back at some of Gonzaga’s best moments, top opponents and closest calls from a streak of season-opening wins.

2005: Gonzaga 69, Idaho 60

After the 2003 loss to Saint Joe’s, Gonzaga cruised past Portland State, 98-80, in 2004 in the first-ever game at McCarthey Athletic Center. Just one year later, the streak was already in jeopardy.

Hosting an Idaho team that would win just three Division I games during a 4-25 season, turnover-prone Gonzaga trailed 34-33 at halftime. The Zags found their rhythm in the second half, building an 11-point lead on Morrison’s 3-pointer with 12 minutes remaining.

But the Vandals continued to fight and Tanoris Shepard’s 3-pointer pulled them within two points with just under five minutes to play.

J.P. Batista, Gonzaga’s leading scorer and rebounder that night with 23 points and nine rebounds, answered with baskets on three of the team’s next four possessions and the Vandals were limited to just three points in the final three minutes.

2020: Gonzaga 102, Kansas 90

Outside of a close call against Eastern Washington in 2011, Gonzaga didn’t face much resistance in season openers between 2005-20 but expected a lot of it playing Kansas in a neutral-site game to start the 2020-21 season.

Both teams opened the year inside the top 10 of the Associated Press poll – Gonzaga at No. 1, Kansas at No. 6 – and both rosters were loaded with NBA talent in a game pitting the Zags’ Jalen Suggs, Andrew Nembhard, Corey Kispert and Drew Timme against the Jayhawks’ Christian Braun, Jalen Wilson and Ochai Agbaji.

Gonzaga opened and closed strong, but Kansas clawed back early in the second half, erasing a double-digit deficit and tying the game at 56-56 on Wilson’s free throw. The Zags survived an injury scare to Suggs and sped off on a 22-7 run late to seal the game and deliver Few’s 600th career win.

Timme (25 points), Suggs (24) and Kispert (23) had 72 combined points for a Gonzaga team that would reel off 31 straight wins before a national championship loss.

2023: Gonzaga 86, Yale 71

A talented group from Yale didn’t necessarily fit the description of “overmatched mid-major” before traveling to Spokane for the 2023-24 opener.

Projected to win the Ivy League and coming off an NIT appearance, Yale assembled one of the best mid-major rosters in the country, featuring a future first-round draft pick in center Danny Wolf and two other players – John Poulakidas and Bez Mbeng – who’d go on to play in the NBA.

Yale’s experience and continuity came in handy early as the Ivy League Bulldogs raced out to a double-digit lead before the first media timeout. Gonzaga responded with a 10-point run to even the score at 16-16 and the teams traded the lead eight times in the first half.

The hosts led by five at halftime and maintained a double-digit advantage for most of the second, stretching the lead to a game-high 21 points late in the half. Braden Huff was one of five double-digit scorers for GU, recording 19 points on 7 of 10 shooting.

Yale lived up to preseason expectations, winning the Ivy League before returning to Spokane five months later to pull off a first-round NCAA Tournament upset of fourth-seeded Auburn.

2024: Gonzaga 101, Baylor 63

Gonzaga had won a handful of season openers by massive point margins, but never against an opponent with the coaching, quality or pedigree of Baylor.

A closely contested game was expected from teams ranked No. 6 (Gonzaga) and No. 8 (Baylor) in the preseason poll and betting services listed Few’s team as a six-point favorite at Numerica Veterans Arena.

Baylor scored first on Norchad Omier’s free throw, but a Gonzaga avalanche followed. The Bulldogs rattled off eight straight points, rode Dusty Stromer’s hot 3-point shooting and established their first double-digit lead on a layup from Huff.

Gonzaga had a 49-30 lead by halftime and continued to pulverize Baylor in the second half, stretching the advantage to a game-high 38 points just before the final buzzer. Five Gonzaga players finished in double figures, but Nolan Hickman led the bunch with 17 points while Ryan Nembhard totaled 11 assists.

2026: Gonzaga 78, Purdue 72

Most Gonzaga fans probably don’t need a refresher on how Few’s team pulled out its 23rd straight season-opening win three days ago.

The 15th-ranked Zags led for 35 minutes and looked like the better team throughout, but some clutch free throw shooting – and an untimely offensive drought from Purdue – were required down the stretch to scrape out the first win of the season.

Davis Fogle was Gonzaga’s leader with 22 points, matched by Purdue center Daniel Jacobsen, who could’ve had an even bigger night without foul trouble in the second half.

Making his Gonzaga debut, point guard Xaivian Lee was the second-leading scorer with 18 points and the Florida transfer delivered three important free throws in the closing minutes to help seal the victory.
