Gonzaga.title: Five-star guard, top-ranked Washington prospect Jalen Davis names Gonzaga in final four
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga remains in the picture for one of the top prospects in the 2027 high school recruiting class.

Combo guard Jalen Davis, a five-star recruit from Bremerton considered to be the top high school player in Washington, named Gonzaga as one of his four finalists just days before an official visit to Spokane for Saturday’s home opener against New Mexico State.

Davis is also considering Washington, UCLA and North Carolina, he told On3.com’s Joe Tipton. The guard doesn’t currently have a commitment date set, according to Tipton.

Davis previously unveiled a list of 10 schools, featuring Gonzaga, UCLA, Washington, Stanford, Texas Tech, USC, Iowa, TCU, BYU and Ole Miss.

The Bremerton High standout is the No. 21 overall recruit in the high school class of 2027, according to the Rivals Industry Ranking that averages ratings from three major recruiting services: Rivals, ESPN and 247Sports.

Davis is also considered the No. 7 player at his position by On3/Rivals, which lists the 6-foot-4 prospect as a point guard.

“Davis has positional size, but he is also comfortable on or off the ball,” On3’s Jamie Shaw wrote in an evaluation of Davis. “With his length, he has some sneaky speed with the ball in his hands and can really put pressure on the defense in the open floor. He is also a quality shooter from 3-point range.

“As he cleans up his footwork and continues to work on his reads, there is real upside here with his natural abilities and physical gifts.”

Davis had a strong summer on the AAU Adidas 3SSB Circuit, averaging Adidas 3SSB Circuit, Davis averaged 24.3 points, 5.6 rebounds, 4.5 assists, and 2.8 steals per game for Slow Grind Elite.

The Zags currently have one player committed in the 2027 class, from five-star combo guard Dooney Johnson, a Milwaukee native who transferred to East River High School in Orlando for his senior season.

Gonzaga.title: 'Thankful' Xaivian Lee delivers in a major way for Gonzaga in Purdue victory | Rewind
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – Gonzaga preserved one streak and ended another by holding off Purdue 78-72 in Monday’s season opener at T-Mobile Arena.

The Bulldogs continue to be a tough out on the first night of the college basketball campaign, picking up their 23rd straight season-opening victory – a streak that goes back to a Nov. 14, 2003, loss to Saint Joseph’s at Madison Square Garden.

In the process, Gonzaga ended a five-game skid against a Purdue program that handed Mark Few’s program three double-digit losses from 2022-24 and won the first two meetings between the schools in 1999 and 2000.

“Apparently (Zach) Edey was the curse,” TNT sideline reporter Allie Force said in a postgame interview with Few, referring to the 7-foot-3 two-time Naismith Trophy winner who had a prominent role on previous Gonzaga scouting reports.

“He was, he was,” Few said.

Xaivian Lee may not have occupied the top spot on Purdue’s scouting report, but the transfer point guard who wasn’t sure if he’d be playing college basketball three months ago leads our first regular-season rewind.

X marks the spot

Lee returned to the Hall of Fame Series one year after starting for Todd Golden and Florida against former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd and Arizona.

The Toronto native scored 14 points on 5 of 17 shooting and 3 of 11 from the 3-point line, pulling down six rebounds and dishing out five assists in Florida’s 93-87 loss.

Lee presumed he wouldn’t get another shot in the Hall of Fame Series – or in college basketball, for that matter – but after a NBA Summer League stint with the Cleveland Cavaliers, the point guard and others around the country began exploring the possibility of a fifth-year waiver. Lee joined a lawsuit in California, securing a preliminary injunction before committing to a Gonzaga program that was desperate for point guard depth after Mario Saint-Supery’s unexpected mid-summer departure.

The former Florida and Princeton player looked like a seamless fit in exhibitions against Arkansas and Lewis-Clark State and delivered for Gonzaga in Monday’s opener, scoring 18 points on 4 of 7 shooting, 3 of 4 from the 3-point line and 7 of 9 from the free -throw line. He had four rebounds, three assists and just one turnover.

“I think it’s kind of poetic that our first game is the exact same as my one last year,” Lee said. “It’s definitely a lot nicer to come out here with a win, but the last couple days I’ve been really thankful to be out here with these guys and playing. I thought today we did a really good job. Obviously we can still get a lot better and I think we will, but we executed pretty well.”

Monday’s debut should be a positive sign, both for Lee and Gonzaga, when accounting for the fact the point guard committed to Few’s program on Aug. 26 and didn’t arrive in Spokane until early September, giving him roughly two months to jell with teammates and learn the playbook before opening against a talented, well-coached Purdue team.

Lee was steering the ship when GU opened up the first double-digit lead in the second half, knocking down a 3-pointer and drawing a foul on another 3-point attempt. He accounted for three of the eight free throws made by GU players inside the final two minutes to help seal the win.

“He’s fast, obviously we were aware of him,” Boilermakers coach Matt Painter said. “I saw him at the (NBA) combine because I went to see a couple of our guys at the Combine. I hadn’t seen him play before. I know that’s crazy, playing at Florida, but I didn’t see him play last year so then I watched tape. His speed, we really wanted to get to him to limit that speed.

“Made three huge 3s. Just like him and (Davis) Fogle, more than anything was keep them off the free throw line. Lee was pretty impressive, 3-to -1 assist-to-turnover ratio, 4-for-7 (from the field), 3-for-4 (on 3s), but the 7-for-9 from the line, that’s where we felt like they just did a better job being aggressive and being able to draw those fouls.”

Almansa to the rescue

Gonzaga’s frontcourt faced not one, but two troubling developments in the first half.

Matched up with 7-foot-4 Purdue center Daniel Jacobsen, Massamba Diop struggled to defend without fouling and the Arizona State transfer was bench-bound after picking up his second foul with four minutes left in the opening frame. Fellow frontcourt starter Braden Huff, meanwhile, dealt with his own issues. Huff missed five of his first seven looks and struggled to convert the short floaters and push shots that usually drop at a near-automatic rate.

Enter backup forward Izan Almansa.

The Spanish forward who became eligible just 10 days earlier was Gonzaga’s most effective big in many ways, providing 29 quality minutes off the bench in his college debut. Almansa was GU’s top bench scorer with 11 points, making 4 of 6 shots from the field and going 3 of 3 from the free-throw line while adding four rebounds.

“He’s been great, he’s just been a pleasant surprise,” Few said. “Easygoing guy, reminds me so much of Killian Tillie the way he can initiate offense. He’s got just a wonderful feel for the game, you can have him bring the ball up the floor and I think these guys would tell you, players like that are really easy to play with.”

Chaos continues

Few may grow tired of the question eventually, but for now Gonzaga’s coach is still willing to opine on the ongoing 5-in-5 eligibility chaos impacting his program and others around the country.

Gonzaga had two 5-in-5 transfers on the court Monday – Lee and fellow point guard Javon Bennett – and another, wing Chauncey Wiggins, on the bench. Wiggins, a 6-foot-10 sharpshooter who spent three seasons at Clemson and one at Florida State, continues to explore eligibility options after coming up emptyhanded in two separate state lawsuits.

Few was asked Monday how he’s navigated an unprecedented era of college basketball.

“Great, we’re well-educated now on the legal system, on the American justice system,” Few said. “We wake up every day, these guys are practicing with us and they’re wonderful teammates. They’re all graduate students, do a great job in class. They’re very, very good players and the exact type of players we want in college basketball.”

Gonzaga’s coach has been outspoken on the topic, reiterating Monday the high school class of 2022 should be grandfathered into the NCAA’s new 5-in-5 eligibility model.

“The NCAA screwed up on this deal,” Few said. “They did. We brought it up as coaches. We told them this isn’t the right time. I’m involved with the Protect College Sports Act and that thing’s coming down the pipe here shortly and you’ve just got to be fair and let these ’22s in. So if you’re on the right side of it, I think you always feel good about it and I feel great about it.

“Blessed to have X (Lee) playing, Javon came in and made two huge free throws there and when we get Chauncey, look out because he’s a heckuva player.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga navigates highs and lows to emerge with 78-72 victory in season opener against Purdue
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – It isn’t hard to draw parallels between Gonzaga’s unique offseason and Monday’s season-opening victory against Purdue.

Both were suspenseful, required some late magic and somehow came together in the end, even when things weren’t always looking promising.

It was a seesaw battle for about 25 minutes between the Bulldogs and Boilermakers, who swapped the lead nine times through the first half at T-Mobile Arena. Gonzaga established an 11-point lead, almost coughed it up and emerged with the program’s first victory over Purdue in six tries, winning 78-72 in front of a split crowd in Las Vegas.

“I thought we played with great poise,” Gonzaga coach Mark Few said. “We talk about, that’s what we have to toughen up, both mentally and physically. That was a really, really hard-fought, physical game. Just what we expected. Down the stretch, we really dug out some stops, we dug out some tough rebounds and we got the ball to the right spot.”

Neither team took control – or led by more than two possessions – until starting point guard Xaivian Lee and reserve forward Izan Almansa combined for 13 points during a 15-6 second-half run that stretched Gonzaga’s lead out to 10 points with 12 minutes, 51 seconds remaining.

The Zags weren’t totally in the clear, though, and Purdue seized control of the game for the next nine minutes, chipping away at the deficit until Antoine West Jr. converted a short jump shot to make it a two-point game with three minutes remaining.

On a career-high scoring night, Gonzaga’s Davis Fogle responded at the other end, driving into the lane before throwing up an off-balanced shot over multiple Purdue players that bounced twice off the rim before falling through the net.

Purdue missed badly on two 3-pointers down the stretch and Gonzaga fared well enough at the charity stripe to ice the game and secure the first win of the season. The Zags finished 26 of 34 (76%) on the night, making 25 of 30 (83.3%) in the second half and going 8 of 10 (80%) in the final two minutes.

“You’ve got to play with poise, you’ve got to take care of the ball, you’ve got to get shots on your term and then just get stops,” Few said. “Mission accomplished.”

Fogle wasn’t always efficient from the field, but the sophomore wing created foul pressure on Purdue all night, finishing with a career-best 22 points on 6 of 18 shooting, 9 of 10 from the free -throw line and 1 of 5 from the 3-point line.

“I think we did a good job closing the game out, making our free throws,” Fogle said. “Just us getting to the line definitely slowed the game down for us and we were able to control our lead.”

Fogle was one of four double-figure scorers for a balanced Gonzaga team that got 18 points from Lee, who finished 4 of 7 from the field, 3 of 4 from the 3-point line and 7 of 9 from the free -throw line in his Zag debut. Almansa had 11 points in his college debut, giving the Zags some much-needed frontcourt production with starter Massamba Diop in foul trouble much of the game. Braden Huff added 10 despite struggling from the field on a 4 of 11 shooting night.

Gonzaga withstood a career-high 22-point outing from 7-foot-4 Purdue center Daniel Jacobsen, who finished 9 of 11 from the field and 4 of 5 from the free -throw line. The Boilermakers struggled when Jacobsen picked up his fourth foul, sending the junior to bench for roughly four minutes in the second half.

“I think three of my fouls were completely unnecessary and I can learn from that,” Jacobsen said. “Be a lot more disciplined, staying down, keeping my arms straight up and stay on the floor.”

Few identified the rebounding battle as a major key for Gonzaga entering Monday’s opener. The Zags won there, maintaining a 34-31 advantage on the glass and a 10-7 edge in offensive rebounding.

A Gonzaga team coming off the two worst 3-point shooting seasons of the Few era finished 6 of 16 (37.5%) from the 3-point line and, just as importantly, held a capable Purdue team to 5 of 21 (23.8%).

The Zags lost to the Boilermakers by double figures three times over a 20-month span from 2022-24 and dropped two other meetings during the 1999 and 2000 seasons.

Gonzaga.title: No. 15 Gonzaga opens season with first win over Purdue | Recap and highlights
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – For about 25 minutes, it was a seesaw battle between 15th-ranked Gonzaga and Purdue in Monday’s season opener at T-Mobile Arena.

The Bulldogs and Boilermakers traded the lead nine times in the first half – neither able to gain any real separation until a scoring flurry from Gonzaga pushed Mark Few’s team out to a 10-point lead in the second half.

Xaivian Lee and Izan Almansa combined for 13 of 15 points during a key second-half run and Gonzaga held off a late push from Purdue, allowing the Bulldogs to prevail 78-72 and pick up the program’s first victory over the Boilermakers.

Gonzaga had scoring contributions across the board, but Davis Fogle led the Bulldogs with 22 points, making 6 of 18 shots from the field while going 9 of 10 from the free throw line.

Lee, who joined Gonzaga’s roster in late August as a fifth-year transfer, added 18 points on 4 of 7 from the field and 7 of 9 from the free throw line. Almansa supplied 11 points off the bench and Braden Huff added 10 points to go with a game-high seven rebounds.

Gonzaga stretched the lead to a game-high 11 points in the second half, but Purdue clawed back with a 10-2 scoring run and closed the deficit to two points on Antoine West Jr.’s jumper in the paint.

Fogle got a layup to rattle in on the next possession and the sophomore wing made three of Gonzaga’s eight free throws inside the final two minutes to ice the victory.

The Bulldogs withstood a career-high outing from 7-foot-4 Purdue center Daniel Jacobsen, who had 22 points on 9 of 11 from the field and 4 of 5 from the free throw line.

Gonzaga (1-0) has four days off before returning to McCarthey Athletic Center for Saturday’s home opener against New Mexico State. The Aggies open the season on Tuesday at home against Western New Mexico.

BOXSCORE

Key moments

GU uses foul shots to hold on

Final – Gonzaga 78, Purdue 72: Gonzaga standout Davis Fogle opened his sophomore season with a career day and all but sealed the Bulldogs’ first-ever win over Purdue with clutch foul shots.

Fogle (career-high 22 points) knocked down two free throws to put GU up by five points in the final 30 seconds after the Boilermakers erased a double-digit deficit in the last five minutes and closed to within a possession late.

Fogle missed a tough floater with 50 seconds left. A Purdue 3-pointer was off-target on the other side, but Caden Pierce pulled down a rebound and dunked it to cut GU’s lead to three points with 30 seconds left. Then Fogle drew contact and hit two huge free throws.

Javon Bennett and Xaivian Lee added free throws later for the Zags, who finished 26 of 34 from the foul line.

“I thought we toughened up,” coach Mark Few said during a postgame interview with TNT. “… I thought we played with some pretty good poise.”

Purdue sets up anxious finish

2nd half, 1:51 – Gonzaga 71, Purdue 66: Purdue crept to within two points with a 10-1 run, taking advantage of a string of GU misses and hitting a few clutch shots to set up an anxious finish. GU’s Davis Fogle stopped the bleeding with an incredibly difficult make on an off-balance floater, then hit a free throw to restore a two-possession lead.

Not so fast

2nd half, 4:50 – Gonzaga 67, Purdue 62: After struggling to get much going offensively for a few minutes, the Boilermakers have found a spark. 

They closed a double-digit gap with a 6-0 run. Gicarri Harris had a four-point play and Daniel Jacobsen knocked down a pair of free throws to make things interesting. 

De Sousa gives GU biggest lead

2nd half, 5:48 – Gonzaga 67, Purdue 56: GU newcomer Nathan De Sousa’s first bucket in a Zag uniform was a beauty.

The guard from France sliced into the paint and finished an awkward scoop layup to give the Zags their biggest lead of the game.

The Boilermakers were matching the Zags shot for shot in the first half, but Purdue seems to have lost a step with Daniel Jacobsen in foul trouble while GU’s offense is finding a late flow.

GU settles, stifles Purdue rally

2nd half, 7:58 – Gonzaga 63, Purdue 54: The Boilermakers used a 6-0 spurt to cut the deficit to four points, capitalizing on a GU scoring drought of about three minutes. But the Zags’ defense settled things down and GU’s ballhandlers started aggressively attacking inside to draw fouls.

The Zags have gone nearly five minutes without a field goal, but they’re earning plenty of opportunities at the foul line, where they are 17 of 22 in this one. Purdue went about three minutes without a point as the Zags extended their lead with free throws from Xaivian Lee, Braden Huff and Davis Fogle. Fogle and Lee are leading the team with 17 and 15 points, respectively.

Purdue big man Daniel Jacobsen, who’s been the team’s most effective player, has spent much of the second half on the bench in foul trouble.

Zag lead hits double digits

2nd half, 11:57 – Gonzaga 56, Purdue 48 – Izan Almansa, the former pro from Spain, continues to impress in his GU debut.

The 6-10 forward fought through contact and converted a layup, drawing a foul and finishing the three-point play to put GU up 56-46 before the Boilermakers answered with another jump hook from 7-footer Daniel Jacobsen. 

Almansa now has 11 points of 4 of 6 shooting, joining two other Zags in double figures.

Quick burst extends GU lead

2nd half, 14:50 – Gonzaga 51, Purdue 42: In a blink the Zags opened up a game-high nine-point lead.

Izan Almansa hit a pair of free throws, then Purdue answered with a jumper before Almansa’s second jam of the game. Xaivian Lee rebounded a Boilermaker miss on the other end, then drilled a stepback 3-pointer, igniting the Zag bench and the large contingent of GU supporters in Vegas.

The two Zag newcomers are looking like very solid additions.

Purdue big man creates matchup problems

2nd half, 15:59 – Gonzaga 44, Purdue 40: Purdue’s offense is revolving around 7-footer Daniel Jacobsen, who put in three straight shots from close range. But Jacobsen just went to the bench with his third foul, which could be a major development.

The Zags haven’t scored a field goal over the last 2:40, but they’re moving the ball inside and drawing fouls, and preserving their lead from the line. Lee is into double figures in his Zag debut after he drove into the paint and drew a goaltend.

Zags take lead into break

Halftime – Gonzaga 36, Purdue 33: An energetic, highly entertaining first half in the season opener ended with the Zags holding a narrow lead after Davis Fogle knocked down a difficult reverse layup in traffic in the final minute.

Neither team led by more than six points and the first half featured nine lead changes. Purdue hit 1 of its last 8 field goals in the half and committed three turnovers over the final three minutes.

The Zags’ 3-point shooting was the difference. They went 5 of 8 compared to Purdue’s 4-for-13 mark from beyond the arc. GU is shooting 15 of 28 (54%) overall and the Boilermakers are 14 of 31 (45%) from the floor. Rebounding and turnovers are about even.

Fogle leads all players with 11 points (5 of 10). Lee has six points on a pair of 3s. Huff has been held to five points on 2 of 5. Pacing Purdue is 7-4 center Daniel Jacobsen (eight points).

GU’s 3-point shooting impresses

1st half, 1:50 – Gonzaga 34, Purdue 33: Outside shooting was an issue for the Zags last year. That doesn’t seem to be the case with this team.

GU is 5 of 8 from 3-point range. Transfer point guard Xaivian Lee is 2 of 2 from deep. He just answered a 3 from Purdue’s Pierce with a contested triple.

The Boilermakers used a 7-0 spurt to take the lead before Lee’s first 3 calmed things down for GU. Transfer guard Javon Bennett, Fogle and Diop also have hit 3s.

The teams are both playing with pace and making extra passes. It’s been a pretty fluid half, despite all the newness on the court for both sides.

Fogle heats up, Zags take lead

1st half, 7:51 – Gonzaga 26, Purdue 23 – Sophomore standout Davis Fogle scored five quick points, including a 3, for the Zags to put them up by a game-high six points, but the Boilermakers halted the mini run. Purdue hit three straight shots.

Huff showed off his fancy footwork to answer a basket from his high school teammate, Purdue’s Caden Pierce.

The Zags are shooting 12 of 19 (63%) from the field. They already have nine assists.

Teams trading buckets in entertaining start

1st half, 11:43 – Gonzaga 16, Purdue 14: Both teams are finding a rhythm offensively, capitalizing on nice feeds to post players. Both teams are shooting 7 of 13 from the field after a fast-paced, back-and-forth stretch. Diop had a nice assist to Braden Huff for a layup, and GU newcomer Izan Almansa, a former Spanish pro, converted on a perfect dish from Huff before jamming a two-handed dunk. But the Boilermakers have answered every basket.

Post players start fast

1st half, 15:54, Gonzaga 6, Purdue 6: Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop, a 7-1 center, knocked down his first bucket in a Zags uniform. And unexpectedly, it wasn’t from close range. Diop drained a 3-pointer for GU’s first basket of the season.

But Purdue big man Daniel Jacobsen answered with back-to-back makes in the paint. Diop responded with a block before a rejection from the 7-4 Jacobsen on a Davis Fogle attempt. The game is tied 6-6 at a timeout at the 15:54 mark. The teams have combined to shoot 5 of 12 in the early goings.

GU’s new-look lineup

The Zags are rolling with three transfers and two returners in their starting lineup.

Their backcourt includes Florida transfer Xaivian Lee, who gained a fifth year of eligibility when a California court granted a temporary restraining order against the NCAA, and Houston transfer Isiah Harwell. Sophomore returner Davis Fogle is starting at wing while senior standout Braden Huff and Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop will occupy the post spots.

Zags looking for first win against Purdue

The college hoops heavyweights have matched up five times before, and Purdue has won them all.

The Boilermakers beat the visiting Zags 83-68 in the teams’ first meeting in November 1998. GU got a rematch the following season in the NCAA Tournament, but the 10th-seeded Zags fell to sixth-seeded Purdue 75-66 in the Sweet 16.

The teams didn’t meet again for over two decades. They squared off in November 2022 at the Phil Knight Legacy tournament in Portland, and 24th-ranked Purdue knocked off No. 6 Gonzaga 84-66 to advance to the tourney championship game.

The next season, the second-ranked Boilermakers, led by star big man Zach Edey, beat GU 73-63 in a Maui Invitational quarterfinal game in November. The most recent meeting came during the same season, in the Sweet 16 of the 2024 NCAA Tournament, where top-seeded Purdue, again led by Edey, topped fifth-seeded Gonzaga 80-68.

“I’ve been haunted by Zach Edey,” GU coach Mark Few said Monday during a pregame interview on TNT. “I think he’s still in Memphis (with the NBA’s Grizzlies).”

Few talks matchup in pregame interview

The Zags’ Hall of Fame coach discussed his team’s roster rebuild and its big season-opening matchup with the Boilermakers on TNT before the game.

“We’re trying our best,” Few said of GU’s roster makeover. “It’s been challenging, but it’s been fun. It’s been a great group to work with, a lot of positive energy and a bunch of different skill sets. It’s actually been fun.”

“The biggest challenge,” Few said, is making sure the new-look team “plays to our strengths” and finds situational matchups. To earn their first-ever win over Purdue, the Bulldogs need to win a “battle of toughness,” Few said.

”(The Boilermakers) are always so tough and so disciplined and well-coached. You have to beat them. They’re not going to beat themselves.”

Pregame

The time for roster building, transfers, eligibility appeals and speculation is finally behind the Gonzaga men’s basketball team.

Now it’s time to actually play basketball.

The No. 15 Zags tip off their season against Purdue in the Hall of Fame Series tonight at 4:30 p.m. from T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas. The game will be broadcast on TNT.

It’s a matchup that features two of the game’s top coaches in recent Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame inductee Mark Few and Matt Painter, who has led the Boilermakers to 11 straight NCAA Tournaments and was national runner-up in 2024.

Gonzaga will feature a formidable frontcourt with senior power forward Braden Huff back from injury, Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop at center and sophomore Davis Fogle coming off the wing.

The Zags will hope that trio, aided by a new-look backcourt assembled after an offseason of upheaval, will amount to a winning formula. The Zags are 4½-point favorites according to vegasinsider.com.

The Boilermakers are turning the page after an illustrious four-year career from point guard Braden Smith, who graduated from the program as the NCAA career assists leader. Look for 7-foot-4 center Daniel Jacobsen to make a big impact inside.

Gonzaga.title: How defense, rebounding helped Gonzaga hold off Purdue's second-half comeback
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – Gonzaga won a couple of stat categories that frankly have been cornerstones during Purdue’s sustained run of success over the last decade or so.

One of those was rebounding, which hasn’t exactly been Gonzaga’s strong suit leading into Monday’s season opener at T-Mobile Arena.

The other was the 3-point line, where Purdue has been the nation’s best at 38.9% accuracy spanning the last three seasons, followed by four nonpower conference programs.

The 15th-ranked Zags had the upper hand on the boards and limited Purdue to just five made 3-pointers, key factors in a 78-72 victory that was short on aesthetics but long on grit.

“We talked all week about the glass just being huge,” Zags coach Mark Few interjected between answering questions on other topics. “Just watching how hard they weren’t against UConn in that exhibition, we really challenged the guys.”

Gonzaga held a small advantage, 34-31, on the boards, including 10-7 on the offensive end, contributing to an 11-4 edge in second-chance points.

“That hasn’t been a real strength so far for us this fall, that was a real concern,” Few said. “These guys stepped up and got it done.”

Both teams are dealing with significant roster makeovers from last season so it might take a while to determine their strengths this year. Purdue lost its top four scorers while GU returned just two players, Braden Huff and Davis Fogle, who played last season.

The Boilermakers misfired on their first five 3-point attempts, despite getting fairly clean looks. They recovered with four made 3s by the end of the half, but still trailed 36-33, thanks in part to Gonzaga’s 5 of 9 shooting behind the arc.

“I think we were getting great looks, executing really well,” said Purdue guard C.J. Cox, who was 1 of 5 on 3-pointers. “It’s going to fall. We trust our guys. We know we put the work in.”

Both teams were ice cold from distance in the final 20 minutes, combining to make 2 of 15 attempts.

“Well, it didn’t feel like we were going to do that (hold Purdue down from 3) in the first half, but you just have to force them into taking them,” Few said. “They’ll take tough ones if you kind of stay on their bodies. When we did lose them, especially in the first half, they got too much separation and that’s when they made us pay.

“B-Mike (assistant coach Brian Michaelson) kept reminding the guys when we hit our coverages our defense was pretty solid. Down the stretch the game, I think we’ll look back and be really happy with our execution at the end.”

Florida transfer Xaivian Lee made the Zags’ lone 3 in the second half, and it was a big one that extended their lead to 51-42. Trailing by 11, Gicarri Harris connected on the Boilermakers only second-half 3 and it turned into a four-point play when he was fouled by Lee with 5:35 remaining.

“These guys stepped up and got stops,” Fogle said. “Defensively, we let them get to their spots a little bit too much. Second half, they still got to their spots and we forced them into tough shots, tough 2s and we got rebounds we weren’t supposed to get.”

Purdue is a pain to defend with a thick playbook, loaded with counters and bruise-inducing screens. The Boilermakers were solid on 2-pointers – 21 of 34 – but couldn’t overcome 5 of 21 on 3s.

“Matt (Painter, Purdue coach) does just an amazing job with the execution, the speed, physicality,” Few said. “These poor guys (Lee and Fogle seated nearby) are just getting blasted, they need a cold tub on those off-ball screen and on-ball screens. But they kept fighting, and lot of times they got a late contest which really makes a big difference.”

Purdue had a chance to make things very interesting in crunch time but missed its last five 3-point attempts.

“We get three really good looks in the last three, four minutes, open 3-pointers and we shoot airballs,” Painter said. “I don’t know if it was fatigue or concentration or both, but that’s your goal. When you take good shots, as a coach you live with that.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga transfer guard Xaivian Lee makes instant impact in first game | Three takeaways
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – Three takeaways at the buzzer from No. 15 Gonzaga’s 78-72 win over Purdue in the season opener Monday at T-Mobile Arena.

Lee shines in first GU game

Xaivian Lee made a big impact in his first official game in a Zag uniform. The Zags’ starting point guard had an excellent shooting night going before missing a free throw with 10:13 remaining. Until that miss, he was 4 of 4 from the field, including 3 of 4 on 3-pointers, and had made all four of his free throws.

Lee, who transferred from Florida after three seasons at Princeton, came through during a couple of key segments of the game to help the Zags win a hard-fought season opener against the Boilermakers.

He didn’t score his first points until roughly 5:30 left in the opening half. His 3-pointer gave GU the lead 31-30. He soon added another 3 to erase a brief Purdue lead.

Lee nailed three free throws, a 3-pointer and an assist to fuel an 11-2 run that gave Gonzaga some breathing room with a 51-42 lead with 14:52 remaining.

Lee ended up with 18 points on 4-of-7 shooting to go with four rebounds and three assists.

Huff’s return

Braden Huff, sidelined after the Jan. 8th Santa Clara game last year with a dislocated kneecap, didn’t have his usual soft touch around the rim in his return.

Huff, often defended by former Glenbard West High (Glen Ellyn, Illinois) teammate Caden Pierce, had several shots pop in and out. He was just 2 of 5 in the opening half. His first bucket in the second half was a tough shot from about 6 feet on the baseline, that pushed GU’s lead to 56-48.

Huff also hit a putback, hiking GU’s lead to 65-56, with 6:47 remaining.

Pierce didn’t do much offensively against Huff, who is three inches taller than the Boilermaker forward. Pierce had seven points and six boards.

Huff, who averaged 17.8 points last season, made 4 of 11 shots and finished with 10 points and seven rebounds.

Up and down debut for Diop

Newcomer Massamba Diop, a 7-foot-1 transfer from Arizona State, scored Gonzaga’s first points of the season on a smooth 3-pointer and added a dunk a few minutes later.

The big man struggled the rest of the half with a pair of turnovers and a pair of fouls. He picked up his third foul 28 seconds into the second half and eventually went to the bench. Purdue 7-4 center Daniel Jacobsen took advantage of Diop’s absence with a couple of interior baskets.

Diop was tagged with his fourth foul with 7:59 left, about a minute after subbing back in. Diop’s final line: 2 of 3 on field goals, seven points and two boards in just 16 minutes.

Diop, who was in foul trouble in GU’s exhibition games against Arkansas and Lewis-Clark State, finished four games with four fouls as a freshman last season. He fouled out once.

Reserve forward Izan Almansa came up big with 11 points and four rebounds in 29 minutes.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women rally behind defense to beat North Dakota State 62-56
Gonzaga.summary:
It hasn’t been often the last couple of years that defense was the most critical element to victory for the Gonzaga women’s basketball team.

The Bulldogs needed all the defense they could muster Monday until they found some offense late.

Gonzaga didn’t get its first lead until midway in the fourth quarter, but it was all Zags until the final buzzer in a 62-56 win over the North Dakota State Bison before 4,464 at McCarthey Athletic Center.

The Zags forced most of NDSU’s 17 turnovers. They pestered Bison shooters often.

Maybe Gonzaga coach Lisa Fortier was prophetic when she had her team do an interesting drill two weeks ago. She said they put bubbles over the baskets to simulate not being able to make shots.

“We put a rebounding bubble on both hoops so that we could see how we responded when the ball wasn’t going in the basket,” Fortier said. “It couldn’t have been more apropos for the way that the game was going. We are such a good offensive team and the ball was not going in the basket.”

The Zags found themselves in a shooting funk for the first 20 minutes. But good starts to both quarters in the second half went far in Gonzaga finding its way offensively the final 20 minutes.

Gonzaga trailed by as many as 11 points in the first half, but found a way to stay within single digits by halftime.

Three times the Zags pulled within a point in the third, but a late surge allowed NDSU to take a 41-34 lead into the final period.

“We were able to guard well enough and not freak out and try to go one on one and do it all by ourselves,” Fortier said. “We were able to contest shots and to rebound. And that carried us until the tie where we obviously knocked down quite a few baskets.”

The No. 1 shooting team in the nation in 3-point percentage last year, Gonzaga struggled mightily from distance. The Zags had made just 2 of 14 before junior guard Teryn Gardner, who stepped into the starting lineup for the first time in her career, gave the crowd something to get loud about.

Gardner hit back-to-back 3-pointers, pulling the Zags into a 45-all tie and then giving Gonzaga its first lead with 5 minutes, 15 seconds remaining in the fourth.

Junior guard Allie Turner took a nice pass over the top of the defense from junior forward Lauren Whittaker and made a 3, pushing Gonzaga to a 57-51 lead with 1:13 to go.

“Defense was a key aspect for us and being able to get over those screens,” said Whittaker, who finished with a double-double – 22 points and 10 rebounds to go with four steals and two assists. “Communication is what really kind of got us through towards the end.”

Gardner, who made 3 of 8 from 3-point range, finished with nine points and four assists.

“People get so many shots up a day (at practice) that you have to keep shooting,” Gardner said. “It’d be a letdown if you stopped shooting.”

Whittaker said there was a simple explanation for the poor first half offensively.

“We were a little bit disjointed,” Whittaker said.

The Zags never found their touch in the opening 20 minutes. The Bulldogs missed their first seven attempts from 3-point range until Gardner converted with 44 seconds to go before halftime, pulling the Zags within 29-22.

The Zags made 10 of 28 from the floor (35.7%) in the first half, but finished 25 of 61 (41%). They made 5 of 18 (27.8%) from behind the arc.

A 3-pointer from Asp Karrington gave the Bison their biggest lead, 21-10, at the 6:49 mark of the second.

Gonzaga senior forward Taylor Smith hit a couple of big shots in the second half, finishing with 10 points and four assists.

NDSU lost two starters to injuries in the first half including fifth-year forward Avery Koenen, who was named the Summit League’s Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year last season. They were on crutches in the second half.

Gonzaga plays the second of three straight at home Friday when Idaho, an NCAA Tournament qualifier last year, visits.

Idaho opened Monday with a 71-47 win over NCAA Division II Saint Martin’s.

Gonzaga.title: Text chat has stoked friendly fire between Braden Huff, Xaivian Lee, Caden Pierce ahead of Gonzaga-Purdue opener
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Glenbard West High School teammates Braden Huff and Caden Pierce had already spent months bantering over text messages about the impending matchup between their Gonzaga and Purdue teams.

It was a fair fight until Aug. 26, when one of Pierce’s ex-teammates at Princeton became Huff’s newest teammate at Gonzaga. Xaivian Lee was thrown into the crosshairs when the point guard committed to Gonzaga, joining Mark Few’s roster as a late 5-in-5 addition. Huff didn’t wait long to create a group text message chat for the three players uniquely connected through different stages of their basketball journeys.

“Right when I committed, they threw me in a group chat,” Lee said. “First thing we talked about was this game. I obviously didn’t know if I was for sure going to be good then, but it’s looking like I’ll be good for that one at least.”

Huff’s relationship with Pierce goes back longer, but recency might give Lee a better idea of what to expect from the Purdue forward when he takes the floor for Matt Painter’s team Monday afternoon at T-Mobile Arena.

Lee and Pierce overlapped for three seasons at Princeton, playing in 91 games for teams that combined to go 91-25 between 2022-25. Pierce was the Ivy League Freshman of the Year in 2022-23 and Player of the Year in 2023-24. Lee came on strong toward the end of his tenure with the Tigers, earning All-Ivy League First Team honors in 2024-25 while averaging 16.9 points, 6.1 rebounds and 5.5 assists.

“Shoot, I might know (Pierce) better than Braden,” Lee joked. “He’s known him longer, but I’ve known him in college. It’s pretty special honestly. But we’ve just got to keep him off the glass. He’s a very talented rebounder and he’s in the right spots, so we’ve got to make sure we get a body on him and obviously pay attention to the scout and know what they’re doing on offense. But really for him, just keeping him off the glass I think.”

There’s a good chance Huff would’ve offered many of the same scouting tips on Pierce.

The Glen Elyn, Illinois , natives have known each other since fifth grade, playing on youth travel teams, the AAU Illinois Wolves and, most recently, the 2021-22 Glenbard West High squad that finished with a 37-1 record and captured the 2022 Illinois High School Association Class 4A title.

After Pierce’s junior season, the 6-foot-7 forward spent a year away from competition to focus on getting an undergraduate economic degree from Princeton. In the meantime, he’d browse transfer options for his final year of basketball eligibility. Gonzaga emerged as one of Pierce’s final five choices – along with Purdue, Duke, UConn and Louisville – and Huff hosted his longtime pal during a Jan. 2 recruiting visit to Spokane.

“That’s my guy,” Huff said. “I’ve known him since elementary school, played since I think fifth grade, we’ve been on a team together. We talked a little bit of trash, tried to get him to come here originally and that fell through. I’m excited for the matchup, I know Xaivian’s got some history too with him at Princeton so it’s going to be a lot of fun to see him and his family after the game.”

Pierce ultimately chose Purdue and renowned coach Matt Painter. Purdue’s campus in West Lafayette, Indiana, is also located just 70 miles northwest of Indianapolis, where Caden’s older brother Alec is a standout wide receiver for the NFL’s Colts.

“I really think (Braden) didn’t want to get too involved because he wanted Caden to make the best decision for him, right?” Huff’s father, Alec, said. “But yeah, I think it obviously would’ve been pretty cool. I think Caden’s super happy where he is, I think it’s a good spot for him but I think it’s going to be a really interesting dynamic when the three of those guys take the court together.”

The two players and their families have stayed close through the years. The Huffs joined the Pierces for one of Alec’s NFL games at Lucas Oil Stadium and traveled to Chapel Hill, North Carolina , in 2019-20 to watch oldest brother Justin Pierce play basketball at North Carolina. Last year, the Pierces returned the favor, accompanying the Huffs to watch Braden and Gonzaga play UCLA at Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle – a trip Alec Huff said was unrelated to Caden’s ongoing recruiting process.

“They’re good buds,” Alec Huff said. “They were in the same social circle, same group of friends in middle school and high school.”

Go figure, Huff and Pierce are also represented by the same agency, Chicago-based Priority Sports. It’s not uncommon for them to train together when both are home in Illinois during the offseason.

The Gonzaga-Purdue matchup was a topic of conversation during workouts this summer and the friendly banter only continued when Lee entered the fold in August. Below Lee’s commitment graphic on Instagram, Pierce commented “what is life.” Lee replied, “see ya in vegas.”

The fifth-year Florida transfer wasn’t sure if he’d be eligible for Monday’s opener, but a recent 5-in-5 ruling in California meant he’d be in the clear for the time being. Since August, Pierce has been taking barbs from both Gonzaga players in the group chat – something that probably feels a little bit like trying to defend a 2-on-1 fastbreak in transition.

“Every time we talk, I tell him we’re going to win,” Lee said. “He’s more humble than I am, so he says nothing really back to me. We definitely have some banter about it.”

Pierce and Lee have particularly fond memories of the 2022-23 season at Princeton, when the 15th-seeded Tigers stunned former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd and second-seeded Arizona in the first round of the NCAA Tournament.

“We were both freshmen on that team,” Lee recalled. “He was rookie of the year, he had like 16 rebounds maybe against Missouri in the second round. We were on a really good team that year, then the next year we kind of both got to run the show a little bit and we were really good that season as well.”

Lee and Huff are both expected to be in Gonzaga’s starting lineup when the ball is tipped on Monday. Pierce, a versatile wing, is on track to do the same after starting in each of Purdue’s three exhibitions.

Huff ’s and Pierce’s community of Glen Ellyn should be well-represented in Vegas. Both families are planning to attend Monday’s game, as is Glenbard West coach Jason Opoka, who faces a win-win/lose-lose situation with former players on both teams.

Huff’s 1-0 record against former Glenbard teammates could be a good omen for Monday. In 2024, he scored 14 points off the bench to help Gonzaga cruise past Bobby Durkin and Davidson, 90-65, at the Battle 4 Atlantis.

“It’s going to be an interesting deal,” Alec said of Monday’s game. “I think that’s going to be an issue for a few people in our community, to be honest with you.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women expect challenge from experienced North Dakota State team
Gonzaga.summary:
When the Gonzaga women’s basketball players step on the court Monday at McCarthey Athletic Center, forgive them if they feel like they’re looking at a team similar to themselves.

In many ways, the Zags will be.

Gonzaga takes on North Dakota State on the first day college men’s and women’s teams may play games. Tipoff is at 6 p.m.

The teams met in Gonzaga’s 2025-26 season opener in Fargo, North Dakota – a game the Zags won 81-66.

NDSU went on to win the Summit League championship and finish 29-5 overall. The Bison return five starters and eight letterwinners.

Sound familiar? Gonzaga returns all five starters and five other key returners off a team that was 24-10, won the West Coast Conference title and conference tournament and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

“They’re really, really good,” GU coach Lisa Fortier said. “They’re just as veteran as we are.”

In the opener a year ago, Gonzaga led 60-38 through three quarters before the Bison pulled closer in the final period. Four Zags finished in double-figure scoring, led by Allie Turner with 18 points on 4-of-5 shooting from 3-point range. Zeryhia Aokuso had 14 points, Lauren Whittaker, in her first collegiate game, had 13 and nine rebounds in 18 minutes and Ines Bettencourt added 12 points and four assists.

The Zags will have to keep many eyes on NDSU 6-foot-3 senior forward Avery Koenen, who had 17 to lead the Bison against GU.

Like Whittaker, Koenen is on the Becky Hammon Mid-Major Player of the Year preseason watch list. She was the Summit League Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year. She’s been tabbed as the league’s preseason POY.

“(Koenen) is one of the best in the country,” Fortier said. “She was one of five players in the country who were the Defensive Player of the Year and the Player of the Year. They have really good guards around her.”

Koenen led NDSU in scoring last year, averaging 19.4 points and 10.8 rebounds. She was the only player in the country last year to average at least 19 points, 10 rebounds and shoot 63% or better.

“They’re kind of like us outside of Spokane, right?” Fortier said. “Everybody in Spokane knows how good they are, but other people don’t. We’re going to have to defend their guards who are tough and gritty. They’re feisty. They can shoot it from the perimeter. They’re athletic. Koenen is an issue that you have to address at all times when she’s on the court.”

Fortier says Koenen wins most one-on-one battles with forwards.

“So we’re going to have to dig in,” Fortier said.

The game is the first of three straight home games for the Zags. GU welcomes Idaho, an NCAA Tournament qualifier a year ago, on Friday and UC Riverside visits on Sunday.

Gonzaga.title: How Gonzaga women have bucked the revolving door trend in new era: 'We recruit uniquely'
Gonzaga.summary:
In a time when a premium is placed on player retention and roster rebuilding, we give you the antithesis: Gonzaga women’s basketball.

At the same time college basketball seems to shift with each change in wind direction, Gonzaga coach Lisa Fortier longs for the old days. Back when building a roster began and ended with high school freshmen.

COVID-19 and the recent 5-for-5 eligibility change has thrown wrenches into the formula in which Gonzaga was built on.

Gonzaga desires that its foundation includes high school players. When the program started making a name for itself in the mid -2000s, the Zags were signing high school players. Before Fortier and continuing during her watch, Gonzaga has followed that formula. Recruit and sign high school athletes, take time to develop them and ultimately reap the benefits.

“We recruit uniquely,” Fortier said. “We’ve never been the group that just amasses talent. We’ve tried to find the right pieces to fit in together. And there is some movement … you can only control so much of that. But we take good care of them. We surround them with people you want to hang out with.”

Fortier has seen it up close for two decades. She’s beginning her 13th season as the Zags’ head coach and 20th overall.

It’s not a coincidence that many programs across the nation have had to eschew the once -traditional means of developing and sustaining their teams – through the signing and development of high school players – for quick fixes brought on by graduation or losses in the transfer portal – in hopes of remaining competitive and not falling behind the winning curve.

Gonzaga has stayed ahead of the curve.

Go back two decades when Gonzaga came on the mid-major scene and started giving teams from power conferences all they could handle. The Bulldogs had an occasional transfer back then, but the bedrock of their success has always been homegrown talent.

Along came COVID-19 followed by name, image and likeness – all of which threw recruiting cycles out of whack. Now comes the initiation of the 5-in-5 eligibility model.

“We used to write out on a whiteboard four or five seasons (rosters) and what that looks like,” assistant coach Craig Fortier said.

Gonzaga doesn’t do that anymore.

“What Lisa promotes is ‘Let’s bring in great people that can get better,’ ” Craig said. “And if we can keep them, then they will get better. We’re always going to be excited to have them as long as we can have them. We never want to have somebody that we’re kind of happy when they head out the door.”

Four of five starters on Gonzaga’s Super Seniors team in 2023-24 were prized high school recruits, developed over four or five years. Interestingly, though, it created some roster consternation. The last two recruiting classes have brought in four freshmen, one of whom transferred out this spring. The 2026-27 roster features one freshman. And the Zags have one commitment for the 2027 class.

How many more players Gonzaga will need to bring in next year depends on how many seniors exercise a fifth-year option created with the new eligibility format.

Seniors Taylor Smith, Zeryhia Aokuso and McKynnlie Dalan – each of whom transferred to Gonzaga – may opt to play another year, transfer for their final season or walk away from basketball.

This year’s roster features six juniors who could play three more seasons including this season. Junior Lauren Whittaker, who was listed on the roster as a redshirt freshman a year ago, is now listed as a junior to be in compliance with the new eligibility rule.

Seven of Gonzaga’s 13 players are transfers. No previous roster has had more transfers.

Thankfully most of Gonzaga’s transfers over the years have had at least two years of eligibility and in some cases three and maybe four.

Of the current group of transfers, Dalan could end up playing four at Gonzaga after spending her freshman season at the University of Minnesota. Former Mead three-sport standout Teryn Gardner could spend four years with the Zags.

Fifth-year guard Ines Bettencourt, who hopes a temporary injunction granting her another year eligibility holds up this season, transferred from UConn to Gonzaga two years ago.

This year’s transfers – junior guards Emmy Roach (Rider) and Jocelyn Medina (Denver) – could spend three seasons at Gonzaga.

“So they’ve started to become our guys in our culture because we’ve had them for a while,” Craig Fortier said. “No matter if they’re a transfer or a freshman, the pattern is always going to be development. The more time you get with them, the better generally you’re gonna do. But we’re also trying to be effective and efficient with whatever amount of time we have with them in getting people up to speed with how we want to play and how we think we can help them be the best versions of themselves. That’s always evolving.”

Technically, the Zags have two scholarships available by NCAA rule. But Gonzaga has never had 15 on scholarship at one time.

Gonzaga has a commitment from Gonzaga Prep point guard Aylah Cornwall, who will sign during the early signing period in November. She will essentially fill Bettencourt’s scholarship.

Lisa Fortier says she and her staff continue to recruit for the class of 2027. That’s largely because it’s not known who will exercise a fifth-year option or perhaps transfer. Fortier always wants to have a scholarship in her back pocket.

“We aren’t done with (the 2027 class) yet,” Fortier said. “Most coaches right now are not just taking any high school kid. They have to be a really good fit or a really talented player.”

Gonzaga coaches have been out and about recruiting this fall. The Zags just offered AnnaClaire Bugbee, a 6-2 forward from Mandan, North Dakota, a position in the class of 2028. Bugbee posted a photo of herself with Gonzaga’s coaches on social media recently.

Fortier and her staff are recruiting players for 2028 and 2029.

“We’re recruiting all the time – it never stops,” Fortier said. “Our best players were high school recruits. They are homegrown. That’s a recruiting model we’re comfortable with. It’s hard to place a value on those program kids. You can point to programs like ours where you grow them up, take good care of them and you coach them well. And when they stay they’ll give everything. That’s the kind of people you want on your team – as many of them as you can.”

Gonzaga.title: Loaded Gonzaga women will be team to beat in rebuilt Pac-12
Gonzaga.summary:
The Gonzaga women’s basketball team should discover that many hands make lighter work this season.

Like 10 sets of hands – and maybe a couple more sets depending on the impact of transfers and a freshman.

All five starters return from a team that finished 24-10 and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

Truth is the Bulldogs have seven players capable of starting. And the other three will likely give coach Lisa Fortier pause when it comes to doling out playing time.

The Zags’ abundance of talent begins with 6-foot-3 forward Lauren Whittaker, who broke onto the scene last year as a redshirt freshman and was a force that West Coast Conference teams couldn’t contain. She was named the WCC Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year.

Whittaker is listed as a junior on this year’s roster. Gonzaga is being compliant with the NCAA’s new eligibility rules. Whittaker, who has exhausted a redshirt and used a medical waiver, can play three more years.

She led the Zags with 19.1 points and 10.2 rebounds per game less than a year after having knee surgery. There’s no telling what Whittaker can do with a second year of strength added to her knee.

“It’s been so nice not to rehab anything,” Whittaker said. “I’ve gotten to work a lot on my fitness and stamina. I didn’t really get a summer workout session (last year) because I was just rehabbing the whole time.”

Floating on the perimeter and causing opponents frustration is junior guard Allie Turner, who will start for a third straight season.

An All-WCC first-team selection, Turner was the second-leading 3-point shooter in the nation last season and key to Gonzaga finishing as the top 3-point shooting team, a spot ahead of powerhouse UConn. Turner shot 47.1%, making 89 of 189. The Zags converted 39.2% (244 of 623).

Turner averaged 14.8 points, second best, and 3.5 assists per game.

It was thought Gonzaga would need to replace just one starter. But guard Ines Bettencourt, who graduated last spring, has been granted a fifth season through the NCAA’s new 5-in-5 eligibility model. Bettencourt and 70 other player plaintiffs in the California-based Glancey vs. NCAA lawsuit were granted a preliminary injunction by a California Superior Court judge. She’s still potentially awaiting final clearance from the courts.

A transfer from UConn, Bettencourt, one of Gonzaga’s best defensive players, averaged 6.3 points, 3.4 rebounds and 3.1 assists per game.

Bettencourt became a strong voice among teammates last season. That should continue this season. She’ll get some assistance from Whittaker and Turner.

The Zags’ other two returning starters, seniors Taylor Smith (forward) and Zeryia Aokuso (guard), had flashes of brilliance last season. Smith should be much more effective and dangerous teaming with Whittaker in the high-low sets, and watch for Aokuso to play the point at times and create offense with her ability to get to the rim.

Forward Jaiden Haile, who was named the WCC’s Sixth Woman of the Year as a freshman last year, and junior guard Teryn Gardner played key roles off the bench. They would start for many teams, and don’t be surprised if either steps into a starting role at some point this year.

Senior forward McKynnlie Dalan, junior guard Christabel Osarobo and sophomore Julia Wilson round out the 10 returners. They will be fighting for minutes off the bench.

Joining the Zags are junior transfer guards Emmy Roach (Rider) and Jocelyn Medina (Denver) and freshman forward Abby Lusk, from Pocatello, Idaho. All three had solid minutes at FanFest.

“We have players who can make plays, who can make shots, who can rebound,” Fortier said. “We’re going to be able to play a lot of them and a lot of them are gonna be able to make an impact.”

With a team loaded with experience, preseason practices have allowed the Zags to pick up where they left off.

“We’re still gonna play with two forwards, we’re still gonna run the floor, we’re still gonna shoot a bunch of 3s,” Fortier said. “But within that context it does afford us an opportunity to wiggle a little bit and tinker.”

Gonzaga won’t have any difficulty scoring, and the Zags will look to push the pace whenever they can. But they must cut down on turnovers and improve defensively.

“Defensively we can be a lot better,” Turner said, pointing the finger squarely at herself.

The Zags were ranked 49th by Bart Torvik, whose analytical data is similar to the KenPom rankings in men’s basketball. No other non-Power Four school was represented in Torvik’s top 50.

Gonzaga is heavily favored to win the Pac-12 Conference in its first year in the rebuilt league.

It’s likely just the Pac-12 Tournament winner will earn a berth to the NCAA Tournament. The conference doesn’t have the credentials that the men’s teams have at this point.

The Zags don’t want to just get to the NCAA Tournament, though. They want to do something no other Gonzaga team has done – get to the Elite Eight, if not further.

“Win the conference tournament, make it to postseason and then hopefully get further than a game there this year,” Turner said.

Said Whittaker: “Everyone got a taste of what it’s like to be at the (NCAA) Tournament and everyone wants more. So it’s just elevating from what we had last year. We’ve built that foundation. No excuses. We’ve been together for a year.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga, even in new league, remain title favorites | Pac-12 women
Gonzaga.summary:
Pac-12 women’s basketball most likely will be divided into three tiers in the reconditioned conference.

Gonzaga and San Diego State should occupy the top two spots by season’s end.

Third through sixth – featuring Washington State, Colorado State, Oregon State and Boise State – will be highly competitive but could finish in any order.

And the three lowest places should be decided between Utah State, Fresno State and Texas State.

If Gonzaga plays as advertised, though, the Zags could make it a solo run to a conference championship, creating a fourth tier.

The Zags are expected to carry over their West Coast Conference dominance into the Pac-12.

Gonzaga is ranked No. 49 in the Bart Torvik preseason analytical data – the highest ranking for a non-Power Four conference school. Oregon State is 69th, Colorado State 80th and San Diego State 97th.

Here’s a look at the predicted order of finish:

1. Gonzaga. Easy, easy choice here.

None of the nine conference teams bring back a roster as deep as the Zags. Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who dominated in the WCC and was named the Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year last season, is expected to pick up where she left off. She’s the runaway pick as the Pac-12’s Player of the Year. Whittaker has plenty of support down low. Couple that with a perimeter that features the top 3-point shooting team in the nation a year ago and opponents will have to pick their poison in what they try to defend.

2. San Diego State. The Aztecs cruised to the Mountain West regular-season championship last year, stumbling once in 20 games. They were upset in the conference tournament, but extended their season in the WBIT where they were eliminated in the quarterfinals. SDSU has four of five starters back and add four transfers and three freshmen. The Aztecs finished 27-6 overall, tying the record for most wins in a season.

3. Oregon State. The Beavers can match up with any guards in the conference, but they sorely lack an experienced inside presence. OSU returns WCC All-Conference First Team picks Jenna Villa and Kennedie Shuler, both senior guards. Shuler was named the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and is arguably the best point guard in the conference. Villa, a transfer a year ago from Washington State, averaged 14.9 points in a breakout season.

4. Colorado State. The Rams won the MW Tournament last year, advancing to the NCAA Tournament where they showed well in a 65-62 loss to Michigan State and finished 27-8. CSU returns just one starter and bring in eight players including five transfers. The Rams have thrived in recent seasons on transfers.

5. Washington State. The Cougars have much to prove, but have a strong foundation. They return five starters – six if you count Malia Rudd, who started 20 games as a freshman. Leading the way is senior 5-8 guard Eleonora Villa, a second team All-WCC selection. The Italy native averaged a career-high 16.5 points and 3.6 assists while playing 34.8 minutes a game.

6. Boise State. The Broncos were highly competitive in the MW a year ago, finishing 25-9 overall and 14-6 in league. They must replace four starters. Coach Gordy Presnell begins his 39th season as a head coach, 21st at BSU. He’s six wins shy of 800 (794-392). The retooling will include three transfers and four freshmen.

7. Fresno State. The Bulldogs have much work ahead. They bring back one starter from a team that finished 15-18. The Bulldogs have brought in eight transfers and three freshmen. They get the nod here over Texas State based on playing in a tougher conference previously.

8. Texas State. The Bobcats have the lone new head coach in Chris Kielsmeier. He was previously a head coach at Cleveland State, Wayne State College and Howard Payne. Texas State brings back two starters. Kielsmeier signed eight transfers.

9. Utah State. The Aggies might as well be starting from rock bottom. They lost 18 straight to end last year after a 6-6 start. They return two starters, but wholesale changes are expected with six transfers.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women picked to win new Pac-12; WSU selected sixth | Notebook
Gonzaga.summary:
With five starters and five other returners, it is no surprise that the Gonzaga women’s basketball team was tapped to win the Pac-12 Conference championship in a media poll released Thursday.

The Bulldogs’ top seven scorers return from a team that finished 24-10 and won the West Coast Conference title in its final season in the league.

Oregon State was picked to finish second in the remodeled conference. The Beavers may have been picked second based on their reputation and penchant for postseason success. In the final year of the original Pac-12 (2023-24), they advanced to the Elite Eight.

San Diego State, which won the Mountain West championship last year, was picked third followed by Colorado State, Boise State, Washington State, Fresno State, Texas State and Utah State.

Gonzaga received 16 of 19 first-place votes. Oregon State received one and San Diego State received two.

Colorado State won the MWC Tournament last year and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

WSU returns six players who started at various times. The Cougars have much to prove after stumbling to a 9-25 record last year.

ESPN released its preseason bracketology compiled by Charlie Creme on Monday. Gonzaga is picked as the automatic qualifier from the Pac-12 as a 10 seed. Oregon State and San Diego State are picked in the new 76-team field to play play-in games.

Players to watch

The Pac-12 also released its Preseason Impact List.

Gonzaga junior forward Lauren Whittaker, the WCC Player and Freshman of the Year last season, and junior guard Allie Turner, an All-WCC first-team selection a year ago, were two of 18 players named. Each school was allowed to nominate two players.

Named from WSU are seniors Alex Covill (post) and Eleonora Villa (guard), an All-WCC second-team pick last year.

Former WSU guard Jenna Villa and point guard Kennedie Shuler were selected from Oregon State. Shuler was the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and Villa was a first-team selection.

Add to the list

Gonzaga’s Whittaker was named to two more watch lists.

Whittaker, from Christchurch, New Zealand, is on the Naismith Trophy Women’s College Player of the Year preseason list along with the Katrina McClain Award preseason list. On Tuesday she was named to the Becky Hammon Mid-Major Player of the Year preseason list.

She is one of two Pac-12 players on the Hammon list.

In her first season playing for the Zags a year ago, Whittaker averaged 19.1 points and 10.2 rebounds per game with 649 points and a school-record 348 rebounds.

Coach list

Lisa Fortier, who is entering her 13th season as head coach at Gonzaga, has been named to the Kathy Delaney-Smith Coach of the Year preseason watch list.

Fortier is one of 20 coaches nationally selected to the preseason list. The award is in its fourth season.

She enters the season four wins away from becoming the all-time winningest Gonzaga coach with a 313-84 overall record. That’s a .788 winning percentage. The winningest coach is Kelly Graves (316-136, .699), who is beginning his 13th season at Oregon.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Lauren Whittaker named to watch list for Becky Hammon Award

The star junior was one of 25 players named Wednesday to the watch list for the Becky Hammon Award, which recognizes the best player in the mid-major ranks.

Whittaker captured West Coast Conference Player of the Year honors last year in her first season of college basketball, averaging 19.1 points and 10.2 rebounds per game. The 6-foot-3 New Zealand native shot 53.6% from the field, leading the Zags to the WCC Tournament title and an NCAA Tournament appearance.

Gonzaga.author: Tuck Clarry

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women see plenty of bright spots in exhibition rout of Westmont
Gonzaga.summary:
As exhibitions go, it was true to form.

Dig deeper and it’s clear to see why there’s excitement about two teams that play in McCarthey Athletic Center.

Nearly a month to the day of its first preseason practice, the Gonzaga women’s basketball team showed it was ready to play Tuesday, cruising past the NCAA Division II Westmont College Warriors 84-43 before 4,490.

All 12 available Gonzaga players saw time in the first half, and a freshman made an emphatic debut.

Abby Lusk, the Zags’ lone freshman from Pocatello, Idaho, made the first two shots of her career, both 3-pointers, and had 10 points on 4 of 4 shooting in five minutes.

Impressive considering she had been out a week after spraining an ankle. Coach Lisa Fortier said Lusk was a game-time decision.

“It’s the little things that, like, Little Me dreamed about,” Lusk said of her debut. “Getting your first college baskets. It’s just a surreal moment. Being able to make two (back-to-back 3-pointers) is kind of fun too. Seeing the love and support from the bench and the girls on the court … it was everything I envisioned it being.”

Lusk finished with 12 points and four rebounds in 11 minutes.

“We wanted to get her under the lights and see how she did,” Fortier said. “And she did very well. … I think her parents would have come up if they would have known she was going to play. But we had no idea.”

Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who was the West Coast Conference Player and Freshman of the Year last season, scored Gonzaga’s first basket. Whittaker ate up the smaller Warriors inside in the opening 20 minutes with 16 points on 6-of-8 shooting to go with four rebounds, two assists and two steals. She finished with a game-high 24 points, six rebounds and three assists in 21 minutes.

Four of five starters from a year ago started Tuesday and Mead High graduate and junior guard Teryn Gardner stepped into the lineup, replacing fifth-year guard Ines Bettencourt.

The lone Zag not to play was sophomore forward Jaiden Haile, who was the WCC’s Sixth Woman of the Year last season. She was wearing a boot from an overuse injury. She started shooting in light practice last week.

Every Gonzaga player logged at least 10 minutes.

Another bright spot was the play of senior guard Zeryhia Aokuso. She scored from all areas, finishing with 14 points in 18 minutes.

Gonzaga asserted authority early in the third quarter, using a 7-0 spurt to set the tone. It was the most pleasing stretch for Fortier.

“The thing I liked the most was how we came out in the third,” Fortier said. “Hopefully our team is going to be a team that gets leads and then play from the front versus always coming from behind. We talked at halftime about what our energy was going to look like in the third. I thought it was really good energy, probably our best quarter.”

It was the second game in two days for Westmont, from Santa Barbara, California. The Warriors fell 71-46 at Washington State on Sunday.

Gonzaga opened the season at NDSU last year, winning 81-66.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women show off versatility, experience during Fan Fest scrimmage
Gonzaga.summary:
Most Fan Fest’s are a happy-go-lucky time, nothing more than an opportunity to put the jersey on for the first time and take to the court under the lights.

For the Gonzaga women’s basketball team, Saturday was different. The Zags didn’t just want to go through the motions. Ten of them played in the Fan Fest a year ago and they weren’t happy with the product they put on display.

Yes, the Zags were squaring off against their teammates, their friends. But judging by the competitiveness, it meant something to them.

Few will remember the score or which color prevailed come March. But for the record, Blue, led by Lauren Whittaker, Ines Bettencourt and Teryn Gardner, topped White 42-30 in the 20-minute scrimmage at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Equivalent to half a game, Whittaker, the West Coast Conference Player and Freshman of the Year last season had 12 points, five rebounds, two assists and two steals. Bettencourt, who is seeking a fifth year of eligibility and is presently eligible, had 10 points and Gardner, who is vying for a starting position and more playing time this season, had nine points on 3-of-6 shooting from 3-point range.

Gonzaga was the top 3-point shooting team in the nation, and the Zags will likely be among the leaders again this season. Blue and White combined to make 9 of 18 from distance.

But as the scrimmage showed, the Zags can do a number of things. And there’s much room for improvement. Coach Lisa Fortier, who along with dedicated assistants Stacy Clinesmith, Jordan Green and husband, Craig Fortier, begin their 13th season, will watch the Fan Fest video.

“We’ll go back and see all the problem areas,” Fortier said. “Half the time I was talking to my friends (during the scrimmage). So we’ll definitely go back and watch (the video).”

As she always does at Fan Fest, Fortier left the in-game coaching to her assistants.

“I liked how we were trying to push the ball (in transition), get the ball outletted faster, run the floor harder,” Fortier said. “We’ve done it in a little bit different way in the past where we’ve had the point guard really pass it full court. So last year we got bogged down a little bit with too many dribbles in transition. So I thought our team ran hard and looked to (pass) the ball to people. We didn’t always score in transition, but we’re getting those opportunities.”

Sophomore forward Jaiden Haile sat out, her left foot still in a boot recovering from what she called an overuse injury. She said she expects to be back in two to three weeks.

Eleven of 12 Zags scored. Interestingly, the one who didn’t, junior guard Allie Turner, won the 3-point shooting contest. She edged Gardner. Turner and Gardner led the Zags in 3-point shooting last year.

All three new Zags - freshman Abby Lusk and transfers Emmy Roach and Jocelyn Medina - scored. Roach led with six points.

Bettencourt had an interesting passing partner during the 3-point shooting contest - former UConn teammate Azzi Fudd, the No. 1 draft pick by the Dallas Wings in the 2025 WNBA draft.

All five returning starters made cases for securing their starting job. And Gardner is certainly making a case to be a starter.

“There are people who are more likely (to start) based on their tenure here,” Fortier said. “Last year we ended up starting the same lineup (every game). That’s kind of been our style, but we’re always trying to not have that be a thing. You have to earn it every day in practice and even after you’ve gotten it that doesn’t mean you get it forever.”

Bettencourt thought the Zags did a number of things well Saturday.

“I mean, what is there not to like,” Bettencourt said. “We started off strong with our (drill) competitions - what we can do individually and then in the scrimmage. We were just having fun. It’s always better to be playing in front of a crowd instead of a silent gym and the coaches yelling at us constantly. It was just good to be back in front of the fans.”

That’s why they call it Fan Fest.

Gonzaga.title: Loaded with experience, Gonzaga women appear better than ever ahead of annual Fan Fest
Gonzaga.summary:
When it comes to the Gonzaga women’s basketball team’s Fan Fest, it’s less about execution and more about embracing the moment.

More than anything, it’s the first opportunity for the Zags to wear their uniforms and step onto the court at McCarthey Athletic Center in a pseudo-competitive environment. Just because the Bulldogs aren’t playing a real opponent, playing against each other can bring out the competitive spirit.

After all, teammates don’t like to lose to teammates – whether it’s a table-top game, a 3-point shooting contest or an intrasquad scrimmage.

That alone is reason for a crowd to show up Saturday when things tip off at 2 p.m. and fans can get their first look at the 2026-27 lineup.

Junior point guard Allie Turner, who has started nearly all Gonzaga games since her arrival from St. Louis, Missouri, is looking forward to Fan Fest.

Turner hopes the Zags put forward a better showing than a year ago.

“Hopefully we’re way better than last year,” Turner said of Fan Fest. “I remember some people being like ‘(we) should have moved (Fan Fest) back a few weeks last year.’ But hopefully this year we look like a well-oiled machine out there.”

GU coach Lisa Fortier was told that Turner brought up Fan Fest and her expectation of making a better debut this year.

“It’s funny that Allie brought up Fan Fest. I don’t even remember it to be honest with you,” Fortier said.

Fortier won’t be looking at the final statistics. She doesn’t put much stock in who scores what or who has the most rebounds in a scrimmage.

“The big thing is getting them under the lights,” Fortier said. “It’s good to see where everyone is. For me it’s good for my coaches to get to coach. I sit on the side and rib everybody and take notes.”

Ten of the 13 Zags have suited up for a Fan Fest. It’ll be a new experience for freshman forward Abby Lusk, GU’s lone incoming frosh from Pocatello, Idaho; guard Emmy Roach, a junior transfer from Rider University; and guard Jocelyn Medina, a senior transfer from Denver.

A roster is usually needed for Fan Fest. Not this year. Even returning is graduate guard Ines Bettencourt, who gained a fifth year of eligibility this summer late under the new 5-in-5 eligibility format. So her former uniform number (8) had been assigned to Medina. Bettencourt’s new number is 0.

Former Mead standout Teryn Gardner, who transferred from Boise State last year and made an immediate impact coming off the bench, is looking forward to Fan Fest.

“We have basically the same team back so I think we’re all super excited for that,” Gardner said. “It’s going to be a fun time.”

Gardner said the goal for Fan Fest isn’t anything complicated.

“We want to start solidifying our plays,” she said. “We want to help the three new girls get to know everything and how we run the system and whatnot. We want to have fun but we want to make it a good scrimmage.”

Sophomore forward Jaiden Haile will be sitting on the sideline. She’s still wearing a boot on a foot she injured during the summer. The injury is healing and doesn’t appear to be longterm, Fortier said.

Haile was selected as the West Coast Conference Sixth Woman of the Year last season.

Fortier has been cautious with Haile’s recovery.

A deep roster

It stands to figure Gonzaga will be a much more polished team this year.

But there are questions to be answered. Can GU win a championship in the first year of the rebuilt Pac-12? Can it win an NCAA Tournament game and go further than any previous GU team? With all five starters back, does coach Fortier just roll out the 2025-26 starting lineup? And with five other returners who got quality playing time, how does Fortier divvy up minutes?

Lots of questions and no hurry to come up with answers.

It shouldn’t come as a surprise that Fortier has decided to stay away from concrete specified goals with her team this year.

“We’re not even really setting those in the same way,” Fortier said. “Our team goal is to show up every day in practice. We’re not even putting that (goals) to paper. We talk about the process a lot. I think it does them a disservice to (talk about goals). They may or may not have those in the back of their heads, but we’re not gonna verbalize those things. I believe if we show up every day and try to get better then all of the end is going to take care of itself.”

Fortier is right. There will be much conversation about potential by a number of people – right, wrong or indifferent – so the Zags would do themselves favors by veering away from those conversations.

They know, for example, they’ll have a target on their backs. With essentially the whole team back they can’t help but be picked to win the Pac-12 Conference and advance to the NCAA Tournament.

There will also be talk of the potential to be the best team ever under Fortier and best in school history. But it does the Zags no good to get caught up in those expectations.

Gonzaga is going to be good. The Zags know it. The Bulldogs will be out to stack days together. And that could get them to where they want to go.
