Gonzaga.title: Pac-12 releases women's basketball schedule, setting Gonzaga-WSU clash for season finale
Gonzaga.summary:
From staff reports

The schedule is set for the new-look Pac-12 women’s basketball season.

The Gonzaga and Washington State teams learned the dates of their conference matchups Friday, the Pac-12 announced. The conference is using the same Wednesday/Saturday and Thursday-Sunday schedule as the men’s games, which were announced Wednesday.

There are 16 games for the eight-team conference with each team playing each other home and away.

Gonzaga opens at home against Oregon State on Jan. 6, while Washington State hosts Texas State on Jan. 9. Times and TV information are to be announced.

Conference play concludes on March 6 with Gonzaga hosting WSU at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Gonzaga holds a 14-7 series lead over WSU and won all four meetings while they played in the West Coast Conference the last two years.

Oregon State.title: Questions Following Oregon State Football's 5-2 Start To 2026
Oregon State.summary:
Oregon State are one win away from reaching bowl eligibility in JaMarcus Shephard's first season as head coach after a 48-30 victory against the Washington State Cougars. Of course, we dive into a recap of the action from that contest as Jesse Legree, AJ Newberry, and the rest of the Beavers continue to spearhead a monumental turnaround. Hear audio from Takari Hickle and Trey Glasper about that result.

However, it's also important to note that after the contest, Shephard was quick to offer condolences to the families of the victims of last weeks' tragic shooting in Bend at Silver Rail Elementary.  Hear Shephard's comments, and why they matter to the state and the college football community at-large.

After that, your host Matt Bagley dives into three questions that have arisen in our minds about the Beavers' season following the hot start.

All that, and the five college football games you should watch this week as the Beavers get a bye week to prepare for a road matchup with Fresno State to close the month of October. Go Beavs. 

Music by audionautix.com. All music produced by Jason Shaw on AudionautiX is released under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

Oregon State.title: Jesse Legree Continues To Set Records For Oregon State Football
Oregon State.summary:
En route to a 4-2 record for Oregon State football, true freshman wide receiver Jesse Legree has been one of the most electrifying players in the country.  The Baltimore native became the first Oregon State wide receiver ever to post over 100 receiving yards in six consecutive games, something not even legendary Beavers like Brandin Cooks and Mike Hass were able to do back in their day.

This week on State of the Beavs, we react to the incredible pace that Legree has set for himself while leading the nation in both receiving yards and touchdowns. We'll also react to Oregon State's thorough beatdown of San Diego State by a score of 66-14 this past weekend, which has made fans realize JaMarcus Shephard's talk of chasing a Pac-12 title is more than simply talk.

Ahead of the Oregon State-Washington State contest this week, we'll predict how things might go against Kirby Moore's squad, and look forward to the reunion with former Beavs head coach Trent Bray.

All that, plus the five games that you need to watch in college football this weekend. Go Beavs.

Music by audionautix.com. All music produced by Jason Shaw on AudionautiX is released under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

Oregon State.title: Oregon State Football Looks To Sustain Momentum Against San Diego State
Oregon State.summary:
To start their first conference schedule in the relaunched Pac-12, the Oregon State Beavers picked up a blowout win over Colorado State this past weekend. Braden Atkinson and Jesse Legree continued their impressive run of form and the tight ends also got heavily involved en route to the 56-26 result. Time to review that result and what else worked for JaMarcus Shephard to get his team to a 3-2 record on the year.

This Saturday, the Beavers host a 2-3 San Diego State squad, who are coming off of a dramatic 31-29 win over the Texas State Bobcats. What challenges does Sean Lewis' team present to the Beavers as the Aztecs deal with a mumps outbreak? In addition to our thoughts, you'll hear clips from Shephard's media availability, as well as offensive coordinator Mitch Dahlen and defensive coordinator Mike MacIntyre.

All that, plus a look at the five college football games that Matt Bagley thinks you should watch this weekend. 

Thank you for your support of the show, and as always, Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Oregon State Football Returns to a Pac-12 Schedule
Oregon State.summary:
After a win over the UTEP Miners in El Paso, the Oregon State Beavers are 2-2 under the direction of JaMarcus Shephard. While many Power Conference programs around the nation likely wouldn't be satisfied with that type of start, it's important to keep perspective on the progress made in Shephard's first several months leading the team. 

As your host Matt Bagley looks at that, you'll also hear audio from JaMarcus Shephard's Monday press conference. Oregon State travels to Fort Collins this week for their Pac-12 opener against the Colorado State Rams. 

In between all the football talk, we also take some time to discuss the No. 21 Oregon State men's soccer team with our own John Severs, as they get into the home stretch of the 2026 season.

All that, and a look at the five games that you should watch during your college football weekend. Go Beavs.

Washington State.title: From dogs in cowboy hats to starry nights, WSU DE Matyus McLain loves his new painting hobby
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The first time Matyus McLain sat down to try his new hobby, his mind wandered to his childhood, back when he would battle his younger brother in video games. Matyus and the younger Mason played all kinds of games, and they still do, but one they frequented the most was LEGO Star Wars.

So on this August day, before he kicked off his first season starring at defensive end for Washington State, McLain sat down at his kitchen table, cleared everything off, spun some tunes using Spotify DJ, got his supplies out and got started.

He dipped his paintbrush into yellow paint to paint two characters, into brown to illustrate a background, into red to draw a series of hearts representing health. He may not have been happy with the way the door to the rest of the game turned out – “my depth isn’t awesome,” he says – but after about an hour had passed, he had a final product.

“It’s a great escape because it allows you to relax,” McLain said, “and it’s not you scrolling on your phone, playing video games.”

Since the beginning of fall camp in the summer, McLain has picked up a new hobby: painting. He’s completed about seven pieces so far, he said, everything from the LEGO Star Wars lobby screen to a photo of his dog wearing a cowboy hat to a skyline view with a moon hanging in the distance. Throughout a long and taxing season, McLain has used his new pursuit to get away from the grind, to focus on a new challenge.

Each painting takes him about an hour to an hour and a half, he says, reflecting the care he takes with each work and his desire to keep improving on them. When he sits down at his kitchen table to paint, sometimes he doesn’t do so with a specific idea in mind. He goes with the flow. He knows he isn’t an expert, saying, “I’m not great at it by any means.” But for now, he’s OK with that.

For McLain, who didn’t grow up a particularly artsy kid, where did this come from? The answer isn’t as profound as it may seem. On an off day during the Cougars’ fall camp in August, he said, the idea just came to him. I’m gonna paint something, he remembers telling himself. So he went to Walmart, picked up a set of painting supplies, and painted the LEGO Star Wars scene.

Since then, he’s authored a few pieces of artwork. The painting of his dog Brutus, a black and tan Coonhound, came from a real photo with the pup wearing a cowboy hat. He painted a scene with a tree with a stream of water running underneath. He has another more abstract painting, and for that one, he tried to use duct tape to imprint a line – “but the duct tape didn’t really seal the lines perfect,” he laughed.

“I would, like, lay the duct tape down so that way, I could paint over it and then peel off the duct tape, and it’d be a straight line,” McLain said. “Didn’t go as I imagined.”

When he sits down to paint, McLain has a pretty simple workflow. He uses Apple Music for his tunes, but he wants more of a variety when he paints, and for that he turns to Spotify DJ. That program gives him all kinds of music, from middle school throwbacks to hit Juice WRLD songs. He’s even been hit with some ’60s music, which he isn’t normally into. “The DJ thinks I am,” he chuckled.

In truth, though, the idea didn’t appear in his head like Dom Cobb planted it in the movie “Inception.” He comes from an artistic family. His main inspiration is his great-aunt Robin Peterson, a WSU veterinary school grad in the class of 1980. She does some illustration work, and a few of her pieces hang on the walls of McLain’s apartment. Those helped push the idea into McLain’s head.

Besides, he was around lots of art growing up. McLain’s great grandfather, John Fister, was a carpenter who built a kid-sized picnic table that McLain used to color on as a kid. He also built boxes, chairs and coffee tables. He sold some. Others still live at the McLain residence in nearby Priest River, Idaho, and McLain grew up around those as well.

Matyus’ uncle, Denny McLain, is also a carpenter. And his grandfather on his dad’s side, Tom McLain, is a musician based out of Chewelah. He plays mainly bluegrass, but his repertoire includes far more. “He is a master musician,” said Matyus’ mom, Julianne.

“It plays into the mental fortitude that he has,” Julianne added. “I think that he has a significant amount of mental fortitude, and it’s only grown and developed throughout the years. And I think having space to do extra things … I know in the summertime, it’s often going outside, getting in the river, the lake, and going for a hike or whatever it is that he’s doing. I think this is a different way, because I think they decompress on video games quite a lot. These kids, they enjoy the social connection of video games, and so I think it’s a productive way to increase his mental fortitude.”

“That part doesn’t surprise me,” Peterson added. “He was always just such a happy kid, you know? Not wild and crazy or anything, but always interested, curious about things, and interested and game to do anything. I think his parents helped instill the confidence that it takes to do that kind of stuff and just to do what he’s doing now, and so we’re very proud of him.”

McLain picked up painting in large part to get away from football, to give himself a release that isn’t trying to push back offensive linemen and get home for a sack. That much he has accomplished, and to those who know him best, the process started years back.

When McLain was a junior at Priest River, his wrestling team was at the state tournament meet down in Pocatello. During one match, McLain was trying a move that took him some time to maneuver and get into place, and it took long enough that the referee called him for stalling. He went on to fall in the match. His parents could tell he was frustrated.

Sitting up in the stands, Julianne remembers thinking, What is he going to do? Matyus shook his opponent’s hand, then went to a corner of the Holt Arena dome and sat down for some 45 minutes. After that, he got up and strolled over to the referee. Later, he would relay that he asked the ref what he saw on the stalling sequence. What caused him to call that?

It was an encouraging sight for Julianne, who has always encouraged her children to sit with the frustrating emotions, not fight them. That’s what makes us human. Years later, McLain has experienced his fair share of them playing for the Cougars, who are looking for their first FBS win this weekend against Colorado State, looking to shake off a six-game slide.

“When he says nobody’s giving up – there’s nobody giving up,” Julianne said. “He’s got lots of really strong teammates with really high character around him, and they’re all supporting each other. And I think that’s very accurate of what’s happening. So he’s got a lot of support even in the midst of the frustration.”

When he’s painting, though, McLain feels none of that. It’s just him and the canvas – not his phone, not TV, not video games. He really wants to improve at painting, he said, a nod to the competitive nature that helped him ascend from Priest River to Idaho to Washington State.

“I think it’s just a fun challenge outside of football,” McLain said. “It’s not scrolling on my phone. I get to relax, listen to music, and try to be good at something.”

Washington State.title: Turnovers have often eluded WSU, which has forced only six. How can the Cougars turn that around?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – A steady pitter-patter of rain fell overhead, providing a melancholy soundtrack on top of the locker room at Snapdragon Stadium, the site of Washington State’s latest showing. Jaylen Thomas, the Cougars’ best safety, stood in front of a crimson-and-white backdrop, his white jersey sporting a black stain on his right shoulder and a mix of black and green near the center of his uniform.

It was Halloween night, and things had gotten spooky for the Cougars, who had just dropped a six-point decision to the Aztecs. They made things interesting late in the fourth quarter, scrapping within one score, but their comeback fizzled out with a turnover on downs. They fell to 1-8 with the setback.

Thomas, though, had done his part. He earned the biggest stains on his uniform early in the third quarter, when linebacker Keith Brown tipped a pass into the air, where Thomas reeled it in and returned it 17 yards before he was dragged down deep in SDSU territory. It was his third interception of the season, the most by a Cougar since 2024.

“Keith made his play, and I was just in the right spot at the right time,” Thomas said. “Happened to be under the ball. Trusted myself, and just let my athleticism take over after that.”

One of Thomas’ best attributes is his awareness. In his first season at WSU, he’s leveraged it all kinds of ways: To snare two interceptions against Kansas State, to return one of them for a touchdown. To take a punt back for a touchdown against FCS Duquesne the week after. To break up two other passes in the games since. “I feel like putting in the work now,” he said back in September, “so I can have an easier life later.”

But only moments after describing his interception against SDSU, he used his awareness in a different way. He used it to add this: “Gotta create more takeovers from a defensive standpoint to help the offense start in a better position on the field and just help the team overall, with the turnover battle as well.”

It was a cogent point from Thomas, whose group has struggled to force turnovers this season. In nine games, the Cougars have forced only six turnovers, which is tied for No. 132 of 138 FBS teams. Only two other teams in the country have created fewer. Ahead of WSU’s final stretch of three games, which begins with a home matchup against Colorado State this weekend, it’s becoming a blight on the Cougs’ resume.

Here are the five turnovers that WSU’s defense has forced: Thomas’ two interceptions against Kansas State, Jackquintin Bal’s pick-six against Arizona, a fumble forced by Jirah Leaupepetele and recovered by Khamari Terrell against Fresno State, plus Thomas’ interception against SDSU. The Cougars also get credit for Utah State’s muffed kickoff, which was recovered by linebacker Carsten Reynolds, but strictly speaking, that doesn’t belong to their defense.

With those turnovers, the Cougars have given themselves chances to swing games and eke out wins, but those have not surfaced for this group. Their defense has forced only one turnover in their last four games, and that may not be the whole story from WSU’s recent stretch of setbacks, but goes a decent way in explaining the reasons behind them.

Think about this, which Thomas also seemed to be aware of: The Cougars’ inability to generate turnovers is costing their offense, and even with redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman looking sharp at the controls, that unit has left something to be desired too. WSU currently ranks four spots up from dead last in BCF Toys’ field position rankings, checking in at No. 134 nationally.

Additionally, the Cougars have only started about 7% of drives past their own 40 yard line, which can be traced in large part to their defense’s lack of turnovers.

So what’s behind that pattern? One of the biggest explanations is one number: Eight. That’s WSU’s total sacks this fall, which ranks No. 134 in the country. Only two other teams have brought down opposing quarterbacks less. The Cougars have not registered any sacks in their last three games.

For WSU, it registers as something of a surprising development, especially considering the weapons that defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk have flourished into. McLain has picked up 25 QB pressures, according to Pro Football Focus, which ranks fifth in the Pac-12. But he’s only gotten home for one sack. Zunk has swarmed in for 18 pressures, but he has only two sacks to his name.

It raises the burning question: What gives?

“I think naturally, teams we play do have a plan to get the ball out,” WSU coach Kirby Moore said, “or they’re chipping Matyus and Linus, and so you gotta give them credit as well, and that’s forced them to get the ball out quicker at times. We’ve been close. We had opportunities even in the San Diego State game there, where the quarterback got out, kinda made a late lateral there to the back.”

“We gotta finish,” Moore added. “That’s definitely something that we looked at on the opportunities that we had as well, because a lot of times when you get a sack, it at times can equal a sack-fumble, and you create a turnover.”

Can the Cougars force one or two of those against Colorado State? The Rams may have the country’s worst defense, allowing an average of 45 points per game, but they actually rank No. 18 nationally in turnover margin: plus-6. They’ve lost only 8 turnovers, which is No. 24 in the country and second in the Pac-12.

To earn FBS win No. 1, WSU may have to turn that trend around. The good news for the Cougars is they have a guy who has become pretty skilled at being in the right place at the right time.

“It starts at practice, just taking everything more seriously,” Thomas said after the SDSU game. “Just looking, having some self-reflection and just looking inward. Everybody having the mindset of, ‘what can I do better to help the team?’ I really take that to heart. Try to just focus on what I can control to help the team succeed, and you that’s what we all try to do.”

Washington State.title: 'My mindset is switched': How WSU DT Kaden Beatty is guiding the Cougars through a situation he knows well
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Kaden Beatty remembers the dark days like they just vanished over the horizon. He was in his second and final year at Kent State, where things weren’t just bad. They were miserable.

Back in 2024, Beatty played nearly 400 snaps in six starts for the Golden Flashes, who slogged through loss after loss, blowout after blowout, making things interesting in only two of those setbacks. He got home for a sack against Ball State, which won by two. He surged in for a tackle for loss against Bowling Green, which won by three scores. No matter what he did, no matter how well he played, his team just kept losing.

So, Beatty remembers, he began to feel sorry for himself. His feet started to meander, his mind began to wonder. Can I just get to next season? he thought to himself. Am I gonna leave this place?

“That’s just not how it is here,” Beatty said.

Beatty was referring to this Washington State team, which finds itself in a similar position. The Cougars have won just one game this fall, a blowout win over an FCS club. Since mid-September, the Cougars have lost six straight games, struggling to find anything resembling consistency in coach Kirby Moore’s debut season. They’ve tried all manner of adjustments – Moore took over playcalling duties last month, then changed quarterbacks – and nothing has resulted in a win, going 1-8 overall.

Naturally, that puts the Cougars at risk of splintering in the same ways that those Golden Flashes did. Back then, Beatty remembers, “it was kinda clashing amongst the team, amongst the coaches.” Not the case here in Pullman, he says, explaining that these Cougs have a stronger sense of resolve and resiliency.

Much of that starts with Beatty, one of six captains on this WSU team. In his second season as a Cougar, he has emerged as one of the faces of the program, a vocal leader and a charismatic defensive lineman. During TV timeouts, he’s on the sideline dancing, urging the Gesa Field crowd to match his energy. After his best plays – he has 21 tackles, one for loss – he’s screaming to himself, celebrating with teammates.

If you could make a leader in a lab like you were creating a player in “Madden,” you would probably end up with someone like Beatty, who has used his compelling combination of leadership and physicality and likability to do his part in keeping this WSU team together. He plays a thankless position, often invisible in the chaos at the line of scrimmage, which makes his maturity even more remarkable.

In fact, at halftime of WSU’s win over FCS Duquesne, the Cougars were only up one score. According to defensive end Matyus McLain, the most motivation came from Beatty, whose Kent State team lost to FCS Saint Francis in that 2024 season.

“I met with Kaden during the bye week,” Moore said. “That is a guy who loves football, and so every day when we get the opportunity to go out there between the lines, he’s energizing his teammates. He’s energizing the staff. I think he’s playing at a high level, and so we gotta do that throughout these last three weeks.”

“He’s a great leader,” WSU running back Maxwell Woods said in September. “He’s really like the voice of the team. He’s a guy like you’ll never really know if he’s down, if he’s happy. He always kinda stays at that same energetic level.”

What’s interesting is this: Over the last two years, how has Beatty evolved in his approach to losing seasons? What did that take?

Back at Kent State, where he redshirted during the Golden Flashes’ one-win 2023 season and emerged as a key player during their winless 2024 campaign, he found himself focused on himself. “It was all about me, me, me,” he said. When he thought about the season, his mind drifted to himself: Why is this happening to me? Why am I in this situation?

“And that’s not what it is at all here. It’s bigger than me,” Beatty said. “I feel worse for these fans and worse for this place than I do myself because they’re really rooting for us. They’re getting behind us, and we’re not giving them the product that they want. Tears me apart. So all I can do is the next thing. All I can do is figure out – how can I be better for us? And so that’s all I’m focused on.”

Beatty is right that the Cougars aren’t giving fans the product that they want, and for the first six weeks of the season, his group wasn’t the one at fault. Those honors went to the Cougars’ offense, which failed to beat a single FBS team under quarterback Caden Pinnick, whose struggles made things exponentially difficult on not only his offense, but his team’s defense as well.

As a result, Moore benched Pinnick for redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman, who has looked better than his predecessor in his three starts. But in the Cougars’ last two losses, a home setback to Boise State and a road defeat to San Diego State, their defense has begun to fall behind too.

The Cougars missed 10 tackles against the Aztecs and another 18 against the Broncos. They also didn’t register any sacks in those two games, keeping their season total at just eight. Only three other teams in the country have registered fewer. Beatty may not be an edge rusher, but he bears some of the blame in that department, totaling just one QB pressure in each of his last three outings apiece.

He’s well aware of that. In fact, that’s one reason why Beatty spent last week’s bye week watching tape from his team’s first nine games of the season, doing what he called “self-evaluation.” He examined his performance against the run and against the pass – “and what I could do, really, just my 1/11 on the team to excel and to really help us get these wins,” Beatty said.

How has he fared on that front? According to Pro Football Focus, Beatty has earned an overall defense grade of 55.4, which ranks last among the 13 defenders who have played at least 200 snaps. His run defense has given him a grade of 55.1, second-to-last among qualified defenders, and his pass rush has resulted in a figure of 57.3, the best mark among rotation defensive linemen.

Those numbers may not raise many eyebrows, but it’s also true that PFF grades aren’t perfect, and if you watch WSU games, you know that Beatty usually finds himself in the middle of the Cougars’ best run stops. He’s an irreplaceable part of this WSU defense. His snap count, 308, reflects as much.

He’s playing some of his best football. His team is not. He had something of a similar experience two years ago, and since then, Beatty says, “my mindset is switched.” After a loss earlier this year, he was nearly shaking when he expressed his resolve to be better: “Nobody is more pissed off than this team.”

Will that help WSU take down Colorado State this weekend and earn FBS win No. 1? Maybe. The only thing that’s clear is that Beatty will keep showing up, will keep energizing his teammates, will keep being the kind of leader that this Cougar team needs.

“We’re toughening our skin,” Beatty said. “We’re getting tough right now, and this football team needs it. What doesn’t kill you makes you stronger, like I just said. Those little nicks, those losses, those cuts that we’re getting every single week, we’re gonna heal it, and we’re gonna get stronger from it. We’re gonna excel and be able to get over those obstacles and conquer those mountains.”

Washington State.title: 'This is unacceptable': WSU falls to Duquesne in final moments, 72-71, opening season with three straight losses
Washington State.summary:
Over the weekend, after his Washington State group dropped a close road loss, David Riley went on the radio and succinctly diagnosed one of his team’s problems.

“We gotta have more leadership than that,” Riley said.

He was describing a technical foul that went against the Cougars, who proceeded to lose all momentum, winding up with a narrow loss to High Point and opening their season with two straight losses. In the aftermath of that one, it became clear that to turn things around, WSU would need to improve at responding to adversity.

After Washington State’s latest outing, a 72-71 road loss to Duquesne on Tuesday evening, it appears that much is still a work in progress. After leading for nearly 90% of game, the Cougs gave up the lead in the final seconds on an and-one, and on the other end, they couldn’t win the game as guard Lazerek Houston’s floater missed.

“It’s frustrating because there is a clear progression with our team,” said Riley, whose team allowed Duquesne to shoot 52% from the field in the second half. “We are getting better, but this is unacceptable for us to be losing these kinds of games where we control the whole game.”

WSU, which has now started a season with three straight losses for the first time since 1964, will regret this one in large part because of how much it controlled the game. The Cougs led for a total of 34 minutes, 38 seconds, leading by as many as 11. After retaking the lead midway through the first half on a 3-pointer from Tyler Kropp, who scored 10 points to get on the board for the first time all season, the Cougars didn’t lose the lead again until the final sequence.

That went like this: With about 30 seconds left, the Cougs got an acrobatic finish in traffic from guard Sebastian Akins, who totaled nine points. On the other end, Duquesne forward Kerem Konan drove at WSU freshman forward Mohamed Sankhe, who tried to draw a charge. He was called for a block. Konan completed the and-one at the free-throw line, pushing the Dukes ahead 72-71 with 12 seconds left.

But at that point, Duquesne had only been called for four team fouls in the second half, meaning they had two to give before WSU reached the bonus. So when the Cougars got the ball back, by the time the Dukes had committed two fouls, the visitors only had about five seconds to work with. Out of a timeout, WSU got the ball to Houston, who made a move into the paint but couldn’t finish a tough running floater, drifting to the side.

It was a winnable game for WSU, which had three double-digit scorers: Redshirt freshman wing Jaylen Harrell scored 19 points, Houston tallied 12 and Kropp registered 10. But many of the Cougars’ problems in this loss had more to do with two other categories: fouling and rebounds.

In the second half, WSU was whistled for 14 fouls. That resulted in a deluge of free throws for Duquesne, which converted 15 of 19 chances. Also in the second half, the Cougars gave up seven offensive rebounds, which turned into 11 second-chance points for the Dukes.

Another trend went Duquesne’s way in the second period. WSU lost only five turnovers in the first half, doing well to veer away from one of the most consistent problems the Cougars have faced in Riley’s tenure, which is now in its third year. But in the second stanza, the Cougs coughed it up nine times, leading to 14 points off turnovers.

“That second half, we got away from playing our identity, and I think it’s really obvious when you look at the stats,” Riley said in a postgame radio interview. “They had 40 points in the paint, and we had nine turnovers in the second half. Those two things are gonna kill you every time, especially on the road. We let those turnovers lead to transition points.”

Also complicating things for WSU was an injury to transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, who missed the first two games of the season with a turned ankle he suffered hours before his team’s season opener last week. He made his season debut on Tuesday, starting and playing 22 minutes, but his outing was cut short with about 3½ minutes to play, when he appeared to injure his ankle again.

It was a costly blow for the Cougs, who had gotten six points and five rebounds from Harrison, a do-it-all wing whose athleticism makes a difference on the glass and on defense. When Harrison went down, WSU subbed in transfer big man Ladji Dembele, who has put up these numbers in three games: seven points on 3-for-12 shooting, including 1-for-6 from deep, 11 rebounds, 10 fouls, five turnovers, one block and two steals.

On the year, WSU is now allowing opponents an effective field -goal percentage of 63%, which ranks No. 347 out of 362 Division I teams. The Cougars are also permitting a 2-point shooting percentage of 65%, which is No. 336. Their defensive problems have surfaced most in the second halves. Here are their opponents’ shooting percentages in the second period this season.

• Davidson: 63%

• High Point: 68%

• Duquesne: 52%

Can the Cougars turn that around? They’ll have a chance to earn their first win this weekend, hosting Division II Northwest at 10 a.m. Saturday. After that, they face a neutral-site game against Hawaii, which will provide an opportunity for these Cougars to prove that Riley is right – that they are progressing.

“We’re figuring out who we can trust out there,” Riley said, “and absolutely, we gotta start shorting that (rotation) a little bit too.”Greg Woods can be reached at 509-459-5587 or at gregw@spokesman.com.

Washington State.title: The College Football Playoff is expanding to 24 teams. What does it mean for WSU?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The college football ecosystem changed in a seismic way Monday.

The College Football Playoff is expanding to 24 teams beginning next season, opening up more spots for more teams, but also opening doors to untold amounts of other consequences.

What does it all mean for Washington State? It’s a tricky question, but here are the top ramifications of the CFP’s expansion, which carves out only one guaranteed spot for the highest-ranked Group of 6 team.

Next season, WSU’s nonconference schedule includes a home game against rival Washington (the second-to-last Apple Cup currently under contract), a home matchup against Kansas and a road game against Arizona. Under the new rules set by the CFP’s expansion, one of which requires Power 4 teams to play 10 Power 4 games each season, those games might be in jeopardy for WSU, which is now regarded as a Group of 6 program – but there’s a catch for the Cougars.

For 2027, legacy Pac-12 members WSU and Oregon State will be treated as Power 4 programs, according to a report from CBS Sports. That means the Cougars’ Power 4 games for next season are expected to be safe, and they won’t have to do any short-notice rescheduling.

What is unclear is how WSU and OSU will be treated in 2028 and beyond. If they aren’t regarded as P4 programs, several of the Cougs’ future games could be in jeopardy, including a 2028 road game against Kansas, a 2029 home game against Kansas State, a 2031 home game against Virginia and a 2032 road game against Texas Tech.

Here are the current nonconference schedules of WSU’s Power 4 opponents in 2028 and beyond, which will need to be tweaked.

2028 Washington: vs. WSU, vs. Eastern Washington, vs. UNLV

2028 Kansas: at Hawaii, vs. Lindenwood (FCS), vs. WSU

2029 Kansas State: at WSU, vs. Sam Houston

2031 Virginia: at WSU, vs. Richmond (FCS)

2032 Texas Tech: vs. WSU, vs. Fresno State, at UTEP

If those games don’t come to fruition for the Cougars and if Power 4 teams don’t schedule nonconference games against Group of 6 opponents, their opportunities to bolster their resume become few and far between. G6 teams have a hard enough time making the playoff, appearing only four times since it began in 2014. Can they convince the playoff committee they deserve another spot if their only opponents are other G6 teams and FCS foes?

The CFP’s expansion also casts more doubt on the future of the Apple Cup, which is set to be played in 2027 in Pullman and 2028 in Seattle, but no games are under contract beyond that. In recent days, the Huskies and Cougars have expressed interest in continuing the 118-year series – WSU President Betsy Cantwell indicated as much at a CougsFirst! event in Spokane over the weekend, while UW AD Pat Chun said there is “an intent to try and continue the game on both sides” in a radio interview – but the potential incentive for the series’ continuation is another factor.

The Power 4 Huskies will be required to play 10 P4 games, which means one P4 nonconference game. Would UW, which has placed a high priority on hosting seven home games per year, be interested in scheduling WSU as one of its two remaining games? Power-conference schools usually schedule one FCS game each season, which go a long way in funding FCS programs’ athletic departments. That leaves one open spot, and it’s unclear whether UW would want to schedule WSU to fill it.

Think about it this way from the Huskies’ perspective: If they beat the Cougars, they’ll have done what they’re expected to, which wouldn’t do much to move the needle for their playoff chances. If they lose to the Cougs, their resume would include a loss to a G6 team, which could mean a big hit to their chances. The Apple Cup clearly means a lot to the state of Washington, but it’s also true that UW has a lot more to lose than to gain from the series continuing.

From WSU’s side: A win over UW would do wonders for the Cougars’ resume. A loss wouldn’t do much at all.

The CFP’s expansion to 24 teams creates more wiggle room for losses – if the 24-team field existed in 2024, the CFP announced, it would include teams like 9-3 Colorado and 10-2 Iowa State – so it’s possible neither WSU nor UW would take a big hit from a loss in the Apple Cup.

Another tenet of the CFP’s expansion: The Power 4 leagues have each announced they are ending their conference championship games, a major change to preserve their teams’ chances of making the playoff field. But the Pac-12 has not announced it will follow suit, nor have other G6 conferences, which will have to weigh two factors. Do they keep the conference championship games, which figure to be lucrative broadcast events and help make their champions more clear-cut candidates for the field? Or do they cancel them, which could protect the highest-ranked team but remove a revenue stream?

“I saw the headline. I saw the headline maybe about conference championships getting nixed as well,” WSU coach Kirby Moore said Monday in his weekly news conference. “I don’t think it necessarily changes our path, right? So whether it’s 12, whether it’s 24, our path’s our path, and we gotta focus on that.”

Group of 6 programs like WSU have a better chance of making the playoff, which is opening up 12 more spots. But in the CFP’s 12-year history, only four G5/G6 teams have made the field: Cincinnati in 2021, Boise State in 2025 (the first year of the 12-team format), plus Tulane and James Madison in 2026. Each has lost its first game in the playoff.

Could the Cougars make the playoff one day? It’s possible. But it’s also possible that teams of their ilk face a steeper climb into the 24-team field than the 12-team iteration.

Washington State.title: Boise State and Texas State on top as Broncos churn toward a CFP berth | Pac-12 power rankings for Week 11
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12 football power rankings are published each Sunday on the Hotline and consider both the latest results and season-long performance. Call it an objectively subjective look at the state of the conference. If you’re unhappy with the order, email us at the address below … or play better. For comparative purposes, we have included the placement of each team in last week’s rankings.

The dynamics of the inaugural Pac-12 season have changed dramatically in the past few weeks.

At the mid-October turn, for example, Oregon State looked unbeatable and Utah State looked entirely beatable.

Now? The Beavers have lost back-to-back games, and the Aggies have won two in a row.

A few weeks ago, Texas State was under .500 and facing a steep climb to bowl eligibility.

Now? The Bobcats have won three of four, walloped Oregon State and are churning toward an appearance in the conference title game.

One component has remained fixed: Boise State was the team to beat last month and is the team to beat this month, with a two-game lead in the Pac-12 race and only three weeks left.

And based on the initial College Football Playoff rankings, the Broncos (8-1) are the frontrunner to claim the bid reserved for the top team in the Group of Six.

In that regard, their competitive position strengthened exponentially over the weekend thanks to three results:

• The Broncos steamed to victory at Colorado State.

• Oregon won at Ohio State, thereby adding credibility to Boise State’s narrow early season loss in Eugene.

• And UT-San Antonio, the top team in the American, was beaten soundly by Florida Atlantic, sideswiping what appeared to be Boise State’s chief competitor for the CFP berth.

At this point, the Broncos have a decisive advantage over all other Group of Six teams in ESPN’s strength-of-record rankings, which closely approximate one of the most important metrics used by the CFP selection committee.

Here are the top Group of Six teams in strength of record, which measures how a team performs against its schedule compared to how an average team would fare against the same lineup of opponents.

(With national ranking.)

No. 20: Boise State; No. 30: New Mexico; No. 35: Louisiana Tech; No. 39: North Texas; No. 40: Liberty; No. 42: UTSA

Positions can shift markedly based on a single result. Prior to losing to FAU, for instance, UTSA was within a few spots of Boise State.

It has become increasingly clear that the Broncos control their fate – that by winning out, they will lock up the coveted CFP berth for the second time in three years.

If they lose once? Well, the situation could get dicey.

To the power rankings …

(All times Pacific)

1. Boise State (8-1/5-0)

Result: won at Colorado State 64-38

Next up: vs. Oregon State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: ESPN’s popular “College GameDay” is heading to Boise this week despite Oregon State’s two-game losing streak. It will be the third “GameDay” appearance in the Mountain time zone in the past five weeks, following October stops in Provo and Salt Lake City. (Last week: 1)

2. Texas State (5-4/3-2)

Result: won at Oregon State 42-21

Next up: vs. Fresno State (1 p.m. on the CW)

Comment: Getting easier to both envision the Bobcats facing Boise State for the Pac-12 championship – it would be a rematch of their Halloween thriller – and to wonder what might have been if Texas State hadn’t lost to UTSA and San Diego State by a combined seven points. (Last week: 5)

3. Fresno State (5-4/2-3)

Result: lost at Utah State 17-10

Next up: at Texas State (1 p.m. on the CW)

Comment: The Hotline assumed the Bulldogs, fresh off the win over Oregon State, would have a stopover in Letdown City on their way to Logan. Admittedly, we didn’t count on them getting stuck there overnight. (Last week: 2)

4. Oregon State (5-4/3-2)

Result: lost to Texas State 42-21

Next up: at BSU (3 p.m. on USA)

Comment: That would be 80 points and 992 yards allowed by the Beavers in the past two games. But the bigger issue is the complete collapse of their previously unstoppable offense. (Last week: 3)

5. Utah State (4-5/3-2)

Result: beat Fresno State 17-10

Next up: at San Diego State (6:30 p.m. on USA)

Comment: Coach Bronco Mendenhall is too good for his team to wallow for an entire season. We’re kicking ourselves for thinking otherwise, even for just a few weeks. (Last week: 6)

6. San Diego State (4-5/3-2)

Result: did not play

Next up: vs. Utah State (6:30 p.m. on USA)

Comment: There are two examples, Utah State and Texas State, of teams playing better in November than they did in October. Will the Aztecs be the third? Or will they meander to the finish? (Last week: 4)

7. Colorado State (3-6/1-4)

Result: lost to Boise State 64-38

Next up: at Washington State (7:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: The Rams have the worst total defense and scoring defense in the country, and it’s not even close. How this happened under Jim Mora is one of the most fascinating subplots of the inaugural Pac-12 season. (Last week: 7)

8. WSU (1-8/0-5)

Result: did not play

Next up: vs. Colorado State (7:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: If the Cougars don’t win Saturday, they won’t win until sometime in 2027. Whether that victory comes next September, October or November is anyone’s guess. (Last week: 8)

Washington State.title: Favored by more than a touchdown, WSU set to host Colorado State | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s home game against Colorado State on Saturday night.

What is it?

Fresh off its only bye week of the year, WSU is set to host Colorado State to kick off the final stretch of the season. The Cougars are on a six-game losing streak and heading into Week 11, they’re still looking for their first FBS win of the season. They’re mired in their worst season since 2009, when they finished 1-11.

While the teams have met several times in the last few years, this will be the first meeting between WSU (1-8, 0-5 Pac-12) and CSU (3-6, 1-4) in Pullman since 2022.

Where is it?

Gesa Field at Martin Stadium in Pullman.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 7:30 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

CBS Sports Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

WSU opened as a 91/2-point favorite

How did the Cougars fare last week?

WSU was off last week, enjoying its one and only bye week of the season, a policy in both the rebuilt and traditional Pac-12. The Cougars had the latest bye week in the conference, alongside San Diego State.

The week before, WSU fell in a 26-20 road loss to San Diego State, making the Cougars 0-5 on the road this fall. Coach Kirby Moore’s team made things interesting in the fourth quarter, drawing within one score on a rushing touchdown by quarterback Owen Eshelman, but the visitors’ comeback fizzled out with a turnover on downs later in the fourth frame.

Eshelman and the Cougs’ offense looked OK, but that group again got next to nothing from its rushing attack, which netted only 68 yards and one touchdown – 34 yards from running backs. In nine FBS games, those three tailbacks – Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi – are averaging only 46 yards on 15 carries.

On the other side of the ball, WSU’s defense forced one turnover, an interception from safety Jaylen Thomas on a pass tipped by linebacker Keith Brown. But that was only the Cougars’ sixth forced turnover of the season, which is two spots up from dead last in the country. And for the second straight game, they also did not pick up any sacks, leaving them with just eight on the season – No. 134 of 138 FBS teams.

WSU’s perimeter tackling also led to several big SDSU plays, including two rushing touchdowns from tailback Javion Kinnard, who made WSU defensive backs Jamarey Smith and Khamari Terrell miss on his two scoring plays. In all, the Cougars whiffed on 10 tackles, according to Pro Football Focus. They’ve missed double-digit tackles in six of their eight FBS games.

Scouting Colorado State…

Under first-year head coach Jim Mora and quarterback Hauss Hejny, Colorado State has lost six of its last seven games, in large part due to its defense. The Rams rank last in the country in scoring defense by a wide margin, giving up an average of 44 points per game, and their 542 yards given up per game is also last in the country.

Earlier this year, Mora relieved defensive coordinator Tyson Summers of his playcalling duties midgame. Summers left the field and subsequently the program.

That move has not helped Colorado State’s cause, however. The Rams’ last win was a 56-49 victory over San Diego State in late October, but since then, they’ve dropped games to Utah State and Boise State.

The Rams are coming off a 64-38 loss to first-place Boise State, permitting a total of 669 yards to the Broncos’ offense led by backup quarterback Max Cutforth. In that game, CSU offensive lineman Toriyan Johnson and strength coach Shelton Bynum were seen arguing on the sideline. On the field, the Rams yielded 352 yards rushing and 317 yards passing.

“I’ve been doing this a long time, and I’ve never been involved with something like this,” Mora said after that game. “So it’s disappointing.”

On the season, Colorado State has given up the following point totals: 13, 24, 41, 59, 56, 66, 49, 31, 64. The Rams are also allowing an average of 8.4 yards per play, which is last in the country, as is their percentage of defensive drives that result in touchdowns: 52%.

But even Colorado State’s 10 sacks rank better than WSU’s eight. And the Rams rank first in the conference in both forced fumbles (eight) and interceptions (nine).

On offense, CSU is led by Hejny, who has completed 104 of 159 passes (65%) for 1,391 yards and 16 touchdowns against two interceptions, ranking third in the Pac-12 with 231 passing yards a pop. The Rams’ top tailback is Auburn transfer Durell Robinson, who has registered 104 carries for 449 yards and nine touchdowns, including a 117-yard game against Oregon State and a 66-yard outing against Boise State last weekend. Their top receiver is former Division II transfer RJ Vick, who has posted 32 catches for 463 yards and four touchdowns.

Fellow CSU running back Mel Brown, who transferred from UConn along with Mora, has been limited lately. He played only six snaps against Boise State, and before missing the previous game against Utah State, he logged just 10 snaps against San Diego State.

What happened last time?

WSU and CSU’s last clash came last season in Fort Collins, where the Cougars ground out a 20-3 win, their defense handing the Rams one of their two touchdown-less games that season.

Washington State.title: WSU GETS HOT FROM THREE, BUT FALL AS HIGH POINT DEFENDS HOME COURT
WSU MBB: David Riley | High Point Postgame | 11/7/26
Cougars Fall in Tight Battle at Oregon, 64-57
WSU WBB: Kamie Ethridge | Oregon Postgame | 11/6/26
WSU unwinds in second half in 83-71 loss to High Point, opening season with two straight setbacks
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Since David Riley took over as Washington State’s head coach, his teams have faced all kinds of problems, from defense to turnovers to an unsightly combination of the two.

When things get tight in the second half, and their opponent hits them with a surge of six or seven straight points, Riley’s teams have also struggled to respond. Those sequences have almost always spelled doom for the Cougs.

That was the story of WSU’s 83-71 road loss to High Point on Saturday afternoon, the Cougars’ second straight loss to open the season. It’s also the second straight season WSU has started with two straight setbacks.

“Our interior defense. That was the biggest thing,” said WSU coach David Riley, whose team allowed High Point to shoot 58% from the field. “We didn’t guard the ball, and when we did, we fouled. You’re not gonna win on the road against an NCAA Tournament team when you give up that many free throws, when you let them shoot 68% from the field in the second half. Our defense just wasn’t good enough.”

Transfer guard Lazerek Houston poured in a game-best 31 points and wing Jaylen Harrell posted 18 for the Cougars, who took a 52-50 lead midway through the second half on a long triple from guard RJ Jones, who totaled 12 points. But on the next possession, Jones was whistled for a technical foul, slowing the flow of the game and taking away momentum from WSU.

High Point followed with a 10-2 run, seizing control of the game, and Washington State didn’t have the horses to respond. The Cougars, who converted 12 of 26 shots from beyond the arc, kept things within five and six points for the next several minutes. But when the Panthers widened their lead to double digits, the visitors couldn’t bring it back.

“We gotta learn how to handle success better,” Riley said. “We hit a couple shots, we’re flowing, and all of a sudden, after that, they started getting to the rim at will. We can’t get distracted, and in a game like this, we gotta have more leadership than that. That can’t happen.”

Riley’s teams have not been known for their defense. In the Cougars’ season-opening loss to Davidson at the beginning of the week, they allowed the Wildcats to shoot 55% from the field, including 63% in the second half. On Saturday, they surrendered a similar performance to the Panthers, who followed the Jones technical with a long triple and back-to-back dunks.

Part of the problem at play for WSU was the presence of Houston, who is listed at 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds. He can really fill it up on offense, and he might be the best shot-creator on the team. But because of his lack of size, he makes for an easy target on defense, and High Point took advantage, going right at him. That included a nice game from guard CJ Brown, who tallied 17 points.

The Cougars played a second straight game without key wing transfer Ronnie Harrison, who turned his ankle hours before Monday’s game against Davidson, Riley said. It’s unclear when Harrison might be able to return. Without him, the Cougs are missing one of their best players, a two-way force whose defense could stabilize this group.

Either way, it goes down as a loss for WSU, which returns to action on Tuesday at Duquesne. The Cougars played a solid game in the first half, opening the contest on a 7-0 run and keeping their lead for most of the second half. Houston looked electric all night, knocking down 5 of 8 shots from deep and 9 of 13 overall. It’s clear he will play a key role for this WSU team.

But Houston and Harrell didn’t get much help. Jones hit four triples for 12 points, but outside of that, here are the WSU scorers: Ladji Dembele and Sebastian Akins had three points apiece, while Casey Jones and Fraser Roxburgh posted two points each. Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, who has started each of his team’s two games, has gone scoreless in each.

But in these two second halves, the Cougars have been undone by their defense. They’ll get a chance to turn that around on Tuesday on the road against Duquesne, which moved to 2-0 after holding on for a close win against Division-II Central State (Ohio) on Saturday.

“This is a team that can guard,” Riley said, “and it really is frustrating to see us give up easy shots at the rim. That’s way too high a percentage, and we gotta do better than that.”

Washington State.title: Washington State women's basketball team erupts in second quarter, then stumbles after halftime in loss at Oregon
Washington State.summary:
EUGENE – The Washington State women’s basketball team piled up 28 points during a sparkling second quarter and took a 14-point lead into halftime against the Oregon Ducks. The rest of the game was much less ideal for the Cougars.

WSU lost its rhythm after halftime and stumbled to a 64-57 nonconference loss to Oregon on Friday night at Matthew Knight Arena.

The Cougars (0-2) managed just 21 points in the second half.

WSU outscored the Ducks 28-9 in the second quarter, shooting 60% from the field in the period while limiting the Ducks to 17.6% to build a 36-22 halftime lead.

Oregon (2-0) responded with a 24-11 third quarter and swiped the lead early in the fourth. The Ducks outscored WSU 42-21 after halftime. The Cougs shot 9 of 28 from the field in the second half compared to UO’s 16-for-30 mark (6 of 10 on 3s).

Standout guard Eleonora Villa was WSU’s lone double-figure scorer with 22 points on 6 of 12 shooting. All-Big Ten guard Katie Fiso paced Oregon with 19 points.

WSU finished 36.8% from the field and 4 of 25 (16%) on 3-pointers. Oregon shot 38.7% overall and 8 of 19 (42.1%) from 3-point distance.

Washington State.title: WSU Hits The Road For Their First Road Trip Of The Season
Gardner Minshew reminds reporters how Mike Leach rerouted him from Alabama to WSU
Washington State.summary:
Veteran NFL quarterback Gardner Minshew was recently named the starting quarterback for the Arizona Cardinals.

In a recent press conference, Minshew reminded reporters that he was going to play college football at Alabama, but late coaching legend Mike Leach changed his mind.

“I was going to Alabama to be a third-string and then to be a GA (Graduate Assistant) and coach,” Minshew said. “And I was fired up to do that, it was awesome.”

Before committing to Alabama, Minshew had a conversation with Leach, who was Washington State’s head coach at the time.

“Coach Leach asked do I want to go hold a clipboard or lead the country in passing?,” Minshew recalled.

Leach’s pitch worked to get Minshew to Washington State in 2018, where he threw for the second-most yards in the NCAA.

Minshew ended up throwing for 38 touchdowns and 4,779 yards in one season with Leach, which helped him get selected in the sixth round of the NFL Draft.

Minshew has played in the NFL for eight years, and the veteran quarterback credited a lot of his success to Leach.

“I can’t overstate what going to Washington State and playing for Coach Leach did for me,” Minshew said.

BERKELEY, Calif. – The Washington State women fell behind by double digits in the second quarter and absorbed a big loss in a nonconference season opener between former Pac-12 foes.

The California Golden Bears started to separate just before halftime and pulled away for an 80-58 win over the Cougars on Monday night at Haas Pavilion.

WSU trimmed the deficit to eight points midway through the third quarter, but Cal responded with a 12-2 run.

Washington State.title: WSU opens season with 76-61 loss to Davidson, dropping season-opener for second straight year
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – These days, college basketball seasons always arrive with an alluring sense of promise. The slate is clean, the roster is new, and the coach talks about how much he learned from last year and how different things will be in this one.

At Washington State, these last two years have started like that. Coach David Riley has talked with optimism about what he learned from his first season, then his second. He’s felt better about each roster he’s had, he says. Each October, he’s vowed to play better defense and scale back the turnovers.

But the Cougars have not delivered on that kind of potential. Last fall, they opened their season with a home loss to Idaho. And here on Monday night, they began Riley’s third season with a home setback to Davidson, walking off the floor as the buzzer rang on a 76-61 defeat.

“This has been the case ever since I’ve been a coach,” Riley said. “You work on things throughout the fall, throughout the summer, you build an identity, then you go to that first exhibition game, the first scrimmage or whatever, and that goes out the window. These guys kind of forget, they lose their mind. You kind of shore it up. You get to the real games. Same thing happens. And I thought this is a great example of that.”

This was about as inauspicious as it gets for the Cougars, who shot just 35% from the floor, including 5 for 24 from beyond the arc. Trailing by as many as 19, WSU allowed Davidson to convert 55% of field goals, including 63% in the second half. Offense was a mud slog for the Cougars. It was like a hot knife through butter for the Wildcats, who sank 12 of their 23 tries from distance, six from returning starting guard Sam Brown.

Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell scored a team-best 13 points for WSU, which used a 10-0 run to make things interesting in the second half, drawing within 47-38. But the Wildcats followed by getting three straight layups, stretching their lead back out to double digits, where it stayed for the remainder of the game.

On offense, the Cougs got lots of good looks. They just couldn’t knock them down. After the game, Riley said this is “one of the best shooting teams I’ve coached,” but it didn’t show: Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips connected on just 2 of 9 shots from deep, Harrell and Wake Forest transfer Sebastian Akins went 1-for-3 and UNLV transfer big man Ladji Dembele misfired on all three he tried. TCU transfer guard RJ Jones also went 0-for-2.

What’s behind those misses? Riley diagnosed the problem by pointing to the way his group couldn’t flow from its first look to an alternative one – the second action, he likes to call them. That was a problem last year’s team dealt with. One game into this season, these Cougars appear to have the same issue.

“It’s like right now in the offense, we freeze up after that first action, and all of a sudden we don’t know where those shots are coming from,” Riley said. “It’s hard to have confidence in those shots. You kinda get a random look, and you’re not ready for it, and I think some of that is just confidence. It’s hard to win when one team shoots 52% from three, and we shot 20.”

WSU played this game without East Texas A&M transfer Ronnie Harrison, who turned his ankle during pregame shootaround, Riley said. Harrison logged a double-double with 23 points and 11 rebounds in the Cougars’ exhibition win over Washington last week, and with his do-it-all skillset, he figures to play a central role on this team. Listed at 6-foot-8 and 228 pounds, Harrison is a senior and a compelling athlete, making his absence a big one for his group.

Riley hopes Harrison can play in WSU’s next game, a road test against High Point on Saturday, but he isn’t sure because the injury happened so soon before Monday’s game. If he’s out again, it’s a serious development for the Cougs, who need his shot-creation abilities and his veteran presence. It’s hard to overstate how big a loss Harrison’s is.

But on Monday, would he have turned a loss into a win? It’s hard to say. The Cougars looked disjointed on both sides of the ball. They gave up too many open triples to the Wildcats, who made offense look easy. Then they missed too many of those looks on offense. WSU has 14 newcomers, which Riley talked about after the game, and it’s not easy jelling that many players into a read-and-react system like Riley’s.

“It was clear we were on our heels a little bit all game,” Riley said. “It looked like a team with a bunch of newcomers playing a team with three returning starters that kinda knew what’s what.”

After the game, Harrell attributed part of this loss to effort, saying, “I feel like our effort wasn’t the way it was…. We practice hard every day. Since the summertime, we’ve been going at each other. We know what it takes to win, and I feel like today we didn’t show what we really had. That wasn’t the team that I play with all year. So we’re gonna get it right.”

That’s certainly not where the Cougars want to be after Game 1, talking about effort. Riley was relayed Harrell’s comments. Did he agree?

“It’s hard to think and play at the same time,” Riley said, “and I think that these guys want to go out there and compete. But when they’re thinking and they’re timid out there because they’re thinking, it looks the way it did.”

WSU has lots of time to turn this around, to make a second-straight season-opening home loss look like an exception to the rule. But it’s not a particularly encouraging start to the season for the Cougars, who now get a road game against a High Point team that won 31 games and made the NCAA Tournament second round last year.

Washington State.title: 5 thoughts from WSU's loss to San Diego State | Rewind
Washington State.summary:
SAN DIEGO – At some point in the fourth quarter, not long after Washington State angled toward mounting a comeback against San Diego State in Saturday’s game, things began to feel a bit eerie.

Driving down the field, the Cougars were facing a 26-14 deficit. Moments later, quarterback Owen Eshelman pulled a read option and jogged untouched into the end zone, letting out a good scream as he did so. All of a sudden, as listless as this WSU effort felt only a few moments prior, the visitors were angling toward a comeback.

It conjured memories of a certain game from two years ago: In 2024, in a road game against San Diego State, the Cougars were looking at a 26-14 hole in the fourth quarter. They made up the ground in the fourth quarter, sandwiching two John Mateer touchdowns around a Buddah Al-Uqdah interception, a string of winning plays to pull off a stunning rally.

These Cougars had no such luck Saturday night. Their final drive petered out around midfield, where right tackle Jaylin Caldwell was called for a false start, coach Kirby Moore took his final timeout to prevent the ensuing 10-second runoff and Eshelman’s final two passes fell incomplete, handing the ball back to the Aztecs.

With six straight loss es, WSU (1-8, 0-5 Pac-12) has three games left to find its first FBS win of the season. The Cougars are idle next week, giving them a chance to rest for the first time after nine games.

Here are five thoughts from the game.

1. WSU has to generate more sacks

After nine games, the Cougars have generated only eight sacks, which ranks No. 134 of 138 FBS teams. That’s not exactly what Moore had in mind when he landed transfers Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk out of the transfer portal last winter. WSU did not produce any sacks in Saturday’s game, the second straight sack-less game the team has played.

This season, McLain and Zunk have had few issues creating havoc in backfields, but the sacks have eluded them. On Saturday, they largely struck out on both fronts. WSU engineered only six pressures on SDSU redshirt freshman quarterback Stone Saunders, according to Pro Football Focus, including two from McLain and one from Zunk.

Simply put: The Cougars have to get more pressure on quarterbacks, and they have to bring them down when they have the chance. On one play in Saturday’s game, cornerback Khamari Terrell had Saunders wrapped up for what looked like an easy sack, but Saunders wiggled free.

2. It’s probably time to abandon the run game altogether

WSU running backs Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi combined for only 34 yards on 14 carries, an average rush of 2.4 yards. Here is how they have fared in eight FBS games this season.

• Washington: 16 carries, 38 yards.

• Kansas State: 17 carries, 72 yards.

• Arizona: 17 carries, 59 yards.

• Fresno State: 12 carries, 45 yards.

• Utah State: 19 carries, 77 yards.

• Oregon State: 13 carries, 26 yards.

• Boise State: 10 carries, 20 yards.

• SDSU: 14 carries, 34 yards.

That comes out to an average of 15 carries for 46 yards, some of the worst numbers in the country. It’s clear the problem comes in large part from the Cougars’ offensive line, which can’t move bodies in short-yardage situations. Maybe that group can solve some things for its final three games of the season, but it’s more likely that WSU can find success by doing away with the running game for the most part.

3. Cougars’ perimeter tackling left a lot to be desired

WSU’s last two opponents, Boise State and San Diego State, were wise to realize something: They couldn’t generate many yards up the middle, where Cougar defensive linemen have done well to bottle things up, but they could very easily bounce to the outside and jet upfield.

That’s how SDSU running back Javion Kinnard scored both of his touchdowns, making WSU defenders like nickelback Jamarey Smith and Jeremiah Bernard miss on his way to the end zone. The Cougars missed 10 tackles in this one, according to PFF, which is better than the 16 they missed against Boise State.

But when you aren’t getting sacks and aren’t generating many turnovers – even with safety Jaylen Thomas’ interception, his third of the year, the Cougs have forced only six turnovers, which is tied for No. 121 nationally – you have to tackle well. WSU has not done so recently.

4. WSU’s offense sustained drives well, but finishing remains elusive

The Cougs converted 9 of 14 third downs in Saturday’s game, an encouraging development to one of the team’s biggest weaknesses all year, which allowed them to sustain several drives. They scored one touchdown on a drive that chewed up nearly five minutes and covered 75 yards, then another on a series that elapsed 6 minutes , 15 seconds and went 64 yards. WSU converted 5 of its first 6 third downs, including two on Eshelman keepers.

But the Cougs couldn’t always finish their long drives. In the third frame, they used up 6:25 to march 40 yards in 13 plays, but on a third-and-10, Eshelman showed his inexperience by committing a costly intentional grounding penalty, resulting in a loss of 14 yards.

That set up a fourth-and-long from the 35, which meant a 53-yard field goal try for kicker Jack Stevens. His attempt went wide left and well short, scuttled by the rainy and windy conditions.

The Cougs also missed a chance to capitalize on Thomas’ interception, which landed their offense at the Aztecs 36. They ran three plays, got to fourth down and couldn’t convert.

5. The bye comes at a good time for WSU

Every coach in America will say the same thing about their team’s bye week: It comes at a good time. But it’s especially true for these Cougars, who will get an extra week to prepare for a home game against Colorado State, which harbors the worst defense in college football.

Theoretically, WSU shouldn’t need much help taking down such a lowly defense, but the Cougars also managed 20 points against an SDSU defense that had given up point totals of 41, 66 and 56. With a week off, look for Moore and the Cougs to make the adjustments they need to earn their first FBS win of the year.

Washington State.title: Dan Doornink, WSU hall of famer and longtime Seahawks running back, dies at 70
Washington State.summary:
Dan Doornink, a standout running back at Wapato High and Washington State University who then went on to an eight-year NFL career that included seven seasons with the Seahawks, has died at the age of 70, the Seahawks announced Sunday.

Doornink gained 1,836 yards with 15 touchdowns in 105 games for Seattle and may be best remembered for gaining 123 yards in a 13-7 wild-card playoff win over the defending Super Bowl champion Los Angeles Raiders at the Kingdome in 1984.

Doornink was affectionately known as “Dr. Dan” or simply “Dr.” for studying at the UW Medical School while playing for the Seahawks.

“I was competing against guys who didn’t have to study all the time,” Doornink once said in an interview with the Times. “It was hard and challenging and I didn’t get much sleep those years.”

After his NFL career ended he earned a Doctor of Medicine degree at UW and went on to a long career practicing internal medicine in Yakima.

Doornink revealed in 2021 that he had endured a long battle with COVID-19 that was made more difficult by a rare blood disorder. He said in an interview that year with the Seattle Times that he was in intensive care for 23 days and lost 38 pounds.

The team’s statement called Doornink “a beloved member of the Seahawks early days, both on and off the field.”

After a standout career at Wapato High, where the field is now named after him, Doornink recalled in a 2018 interview with the Seattle Times that he signed with WSU and then-coach Jim Sweeney as a quarterback. However, he was far down on the depth chart and moved to running back when injuries hit that position.

He led the Cougars in rushing in both 1976 and 1977, the latter season when WSU opened the season with one of the team’s biggest non-conference road wins ever, a 19-10 victory over 15th-ranked Nebraska. Doornink, a member of WSU’s Hall of Fame, remains 14th on the school’s all-time rushing list with 1,739 yards and is also 25th in career receptions with 105.

Taken 174th overall by the Giants in 1978, he rushed for 306 yards as a rookie despite missing six games with a shoulder injury before being traded to the Seahawks shortly before the start of the 1979 season for a 1980 seventh-round pick.

Doornink became a regular starter for the 1979 and 1980 seasons and then a key rotational player in the backfield from 1981-85. His 1,530 yards with the Seahawks is 14th in franchise history which included a career-high 500 in 1979 when Seattle finished 9-7.

He turned in his career regular season single-game high that season with 122 on 21 carries when the Seahawks beat Atlanta on what was the team’s first-ever appearance on Monday Night Football, a game many remember for Jim Zorn throwing a pass for a first down on a fake field goal to kicker Efren Herrera. That was the only 100-yard game of Doornink’s career in the regular season.

However, he would memorably top that number when Seahawks coach Chuck Knox decided to feature him as part of what was something of a surprise offensive attack emphasizing the running game when the Seahawks hosted the Raiders in the wild card round following the 1984 season. Seattle had lost its final two games against the Chiefs and Broncos, the latter contest costing the Seahawks the AFC West title, due in part to committing nine turnovers combined in the two defeats, including eight interceptions.

Knox decided to get back to basics against the Raiders, unveiling a double tight-end formation that the team used almost exclusively, and Seattle ran it 51 times while throwing just 10 in defeating LA. Doornink, who hadn’t had a carry in the previous two games, got handed the ball a career-high 29 times as the Seahawks took a 13-0 lead and held on.

“They knew exactly what we were going to do and still we were able to get th yards,” a happy Doornink said afterward.

Washington State.title: WSU hoops ready to kick off new season with home matchup against Davidson
Washington State.summary:
Earlier this summer, when David Riley was enjoying a break from coaching the Washington State’s men’s basketball team, he got a ribbing from his brother.

Noah Riley, a quality control coach and analyst for the NFL’s New York Giants, gave him a hard time: Our teams are way tougher.

Back then, Noah was likely referring to the two problems that have plagued Riley’s first two WSU teams: Turnovers and defense. The Cougars finished last season ranked No. 292 in turnover rate and No. 248 in effective field goal percentage defense, painting a picture of an undisciplined, mistake-prone club.

Ahead of Riley’s third season at WSU, which begins with a home matchup against Davidson at 6 p.m. Monday, can the Cougars reverse those trends?

“Well, I think it starts in practice,” said Riley, whose team plays just five home nonconference games this season. “With our teams in the past that have won championships and won a lot of games, there’s been chippy practices, and it’s uncomfortable. And you walk away from practice with just a little bit of uncomfortableness because someone had to lose. I think that’s something that we’ve taken away this year.”

In the first year of the rebuilt Pac-12, WSU will use a retooled roster with 14 newcomers to try and turn around the problems that afflicted the last two Cougar teams. As they head into Monday’s season opener, they’ll likely start the same group that fueled their team’s second and final exhibition game, a road win over rival Washington last week.

That will likely mean lots of touches for East Texas A&M transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, who tallied a team-best 23 points and 11 rebounds in that game, plus opportunities for Central Missouri transfer guard Lazerek Houston and Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips, each of whom scored in double figures. The rest of the Cougs’ starting lineup figures to include UNLV transfer big man Ladji Dembele and Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, whose size could make a difference for a WSU team that has struggled to rebound the past two seasons.

Against Davidson, which was picked to finish eighth of 14 teams in the Atlantic 10 preseason poll, WSU will likely need some more of that recipe. The Cougars played an ugly game to beat the Huskies . The game featured a combined 87 free throws, and neither team shot better than 40% from the field . But they did make nine 3-pointers. They got five combined from Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell and former Eastern Washington wing Casey Jones, who spent the last two years on a church mission.

From a 30,000-foot view, that’s the main contingent that the Cougars will use to replace several key offseason losses, including several to the transfer portal: Ace Glass (Vanderbilt), forward ND Okafor (Mississippi State) and wing Ri Vavers (Memphis), plus guards Jerone Morton (Kentucky) and Tomas Thrastarson (Seattle U), forward Eemeli Yalaho (NC State) and key reserve Parker Gerrits (Wyoming).

This WSU team features only two returners, forward Dominik Robinson and walk-on guard Dio Blakely, which means most of the minutes will belong to transfers. A few other names to watch include TCU transfer RJ Jones and French freshman forward Mohamed Sankhe.

Sankhe totaled five points and three rebounds in 15 minutes against UW.

Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins also figures to make a splash, but because an injury sidelined him for both exhibition games, it’s unclear when he’ll be able to get on the court.

“We’ve got a lot of new faces, and so it’s been a really busy preseason for us trying to get in some concepts,” Riley said. “I think we simplified a few things to make sure that we’re able to play together and play hard, and I think that’s something that just takes time. And I think we’re learning those lessons.”
